articles.content:
Christopher Nolan’s smash hit epic has continued to excite and enrage everyone from rightwingers to academics, an old-fashioned throwback to a uniting big-screen event

The Odyssey: jaw-dropping action, dark magic and dolphin cameos – discuss with spoilers

Go woke, get rich: why rightwing hate campaigns don’t affect the box office

I f a high-profile academic is reviewing a movie for the London Review of Books , that movie in question must be making some kind of mark on some kind of culture. And if people are actually reading a movie review in the London Review of Books, and writing thinkpieces in disagreement or favor of said movie or its review, that movie may actually be a cultural phenomenon.

Normally, volume of discourse about a movie should not be mistaken for a sign that people are actually seeing it. Sometimes online factions just have a bored fixation not shared by the rest of the world. But Christopher Nolan ’s The Odyssey has some major receipts at the box office , too: the movie has already outgrossed Oppenheimer, Nolan’s last movie, itself a shockingly popular movie for adults. Though The Odyssey’s audience skewed male in its first weekend, by its second its gender split was closer to 50/50 , suggesting reach beyond the stereotypically male-driven action-adventures. It’s also reaching out to older moviegoers, an endangered demographic in a summer where under-25s have driven the success of Obsession and Backrooms . Three-quarters of The Odyssey’s audience has been over 25, while memes inspired by the movie (most popular: Matt Damon ’s anguished face portraying Odysseus listening to the sirens’ song and Robert Pattinson ’s slimy suitor demanding that “someone get these BEGGARS out of here!”) have indicated that younger people are paying attention too.

All told, The Odyssey fast closing in on a billion dollars worldwide, and the number of movies that have done this without superheroes, sequel hype or a whole lot of animation is vanishingly small. This is the strange, rarified air that Nolan’s film now occupies. Meanwhile, exactly those other types of movies traditionally aiming for that territory – superhero movies such as Supergirl , remakes including Masters of the Universe or Moana , animation films like Toy Story 5 and Minions & Monsters – have failed to catch on more broadly. Some have bombed, some have underperformed and some have become seemingly frictionless billion-dollar smashes , but none feel like true events. Though an incoming mega-smash featuring Spider-Man reinforces that sometimes audiences will still rush out for the right familiar superhero, Nolan’s movie still stands out in a summer that may have seen tides turn against IP.

Of course, The Odyssey is also, in its way, a form of IP; it’s a story that almost everyone purports to at least kinda-sorta know, even if the specifics are lost somewhere in the halls of high school. Nolan’s big-budget adaptation of the Homeric epic has emerged as a towering piece of monoculture that throws back to pre-fragmentation days. Or, at very least, back to less preordained smashes including Barbie or Top Gun: Maverick, IP projects that seem to dig deeper into audiences’ psyche than other, more preordained blockbusters.

Specifically, these kinds of monocultural events stand in opposition to so many 21st-century box office hits that manage to make tons of money while still feeling like a niche. This was pioneered by the Twilight movies , which would make $700m worldwide like clockwork without ever feeling like an all-demographics smash, but there are plenty of hit superhero movies that also qualify: movies that a lot of people who like that sort of thing saw, without convincing infrequent moviegoers (whose infrequency has seemingly only grown post-pandemic) to show up. Even a less expected smash such as A Minecraft Movie isn’t exactly a unifying force across demographics. Call it the difference between Avatar (massive worldwide phenom that seemed to reach across demographics) and Avatar 3 (big hit for the not-insubstantial group of people who have been watching every Avatar movie, but nothing your grandparents likely went out for).

It’s tempting to classify The Odyssey’s cultural success as reminiscent of a pre-internet time, and in some ways it is, befitting its connections to old-fashioned sword-and-sandal epics of the 1950s. Yet it’s really a convergence of old-fashioned monoculture and more newfangled discourse explosion. Rather than a superhero movie generating endless rewritings of the same nerd-to-normie translations (who was that character and are they going to be in the next superhero thing?) and glorified spoilers (is there a post-credits scene? And while we’re at it, can you describe it for me?), here is an R-rated movie, based on an epic poem, aimed at adults, prompting essays from film critics, academics and amateur Nolan scholars. It’s movie discourse fit for a 200-student freshman seminar, writ even larger.

That might sound dismissive in its own way. But as tediously rancorous as the Very Online versions of these discussions can be, fueled by sometimes-insufferable Nolan acolytes and their equally disagreeable opponents, with the bonus unwelcome intrusion of a failed pre-release rightwing culture war , there’s at least a trackable rationality to a lot of post-release Odyssey discourse. Is it even something like ... healthy cultural-studies debate?! At first, the classicist and, most crucially, Odyssey translator Emily Wilson seemed to be forming a surprise backlash (given that Nolan had cited her translation’s opening line as inspiring his work) with her London Review of Books piece, focusing on the director’s deviations from the text, what she sees as thematic inconsistencies and simplifications, and some potential blind spots in race and gender. This then turned into an internet-fueled critique of an academic’s analysis of film, which some felt included some misreadings of certain characters, scenes and ideas.

Some of the exchanges feel like a turf war between classics and film – are academics not encouraged to weigh in on movies using a different framework? Are mainstream film critics not encouraged to defend their sometimes (often) less rigorous discipline from those who feel confident dipping into it because of the subject matter? Other discussions have emerged (or re-emerged) from within the film community, reviving questions about whether the most popular name-brand writer-director in the world gives the short shrift to his female characters. Anne Hathaway ’s Penelope joins her two other Nolan characters, from The Dark Knight Rises and Interstellar, as some of the strongest in his filmography. But it’s undeniable that Nolan tends to characterize his female leads as wives or wife figures, and some have opined that the new movie’s wealth of women feel marginalized in ways they aren’t in the millennia-old original text.

Odyssey debates have touched exhibition, too: is Nolan’s film, shot entirely on IMAX cameras but only available to be shown in that native format in a few dozen theaters worldwide, placing undue emphasis on a more elitist form of spectacle? Or is he simply providing a level of showmanship that causes demand to outstrip a symbolically meager supply?

The sheer volume of back-and-forth can be wearying – even (especially?) for pop-culture writers who make their living generating reviews, essays, thinkpieces and follow-ups off of the biggest hits of the day. Here’s a bummer stat from my own experience: since the beginning of this year’s summer movie season, there have been at least half a dozen discussion-worthy movies I haven’t written about in any great detail, because of middling-to-low demand. On the other hand, I’ve written about The Odyssey and Obsession, this summer’s other major cultural phenom, close to a dozen times put together. I’m grateful for the work – and for the existence of popular movies that can withstand more robust and varied discussion than a 700-word, thumbs-up-or-down review. On the other hand, a new genuine monoculture threatens to simply refine which handful of movies generates 90% of coverage. (At least the “ending explained” industrial complex will have a chance to examine endings that might actually bear analysis, as The Odyssey in particular does.)

What’s most striking about the Odyssey discourse, however, is that even amid some built-in rancor or disdain, people actually seem excited to engage in it, rather than listlessly scrolling through it on their way to the next tempest in a teapot. That hybridization of old-school monoculture and more technologically enhanced saturation – unlike those 1950s epics and real Imax availability notwithstanding, both the movie and discussion of it feels nearly as accessible as a streaming series du jour, and probably more rewarding – doesn’t feel like astroturfing, but an actual post-release excitement that’s rarer and more fun than pre-release hype. (You have to be truly excited to successfully wring memes from the carefully controlled images of a Nolan film.) Even that ginned-up faux-outrage about the movie’s diversity became amusingly sporting with the gradual and merry realization that most people truly do not care about what infuriates Elon Musk . The movie that a vocal minority insisted was bringing about the destruction of the west, or whatever they were prattling on about, has turned out to be a great unifier – not necessarily of opinion, but towards a reminder that going to the movies and talking about them after, rather than casting about for what else is on, can still feel like a vital part of living in the world.

articles.title: Stick to spending limits, PM and chancellor tell ministers in joint memo
articles.summary: The Chancellor said the Budget on 28 October would “meet our fiscal rules” and give families "stability" to plan for the future.
articles.content:
Chancellor John Healey said his first budget would be built around fiscal discipline

Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have written a joint letter to cabinet ministers telling them they must stick within their existing spending limits while funding new pledges.

After taking office, Burnham announced a host of new cost-of-living policies, including scrapping of VAT from domestic electricity bills , reduced business rates for pubs, and capping bus fares in England.

Burnham and Healey are determined to stick within the fiscal rules set out by their predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves, treasury sources have told the BBC.

Healey's first Budget will be on 28 October and will be "built on fiscal discipline", the chancellor said.

Healey said the budget would "meet our fiscal rules" and "give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future".

A report in the Times says the joint letter told ministers they must "within the budgets they have already got" even while "pay[ing] for new things they want to do this year and next".

While the ongoing war in Iran is pushing up inflation and borrowing costs, senior Treasury sources confirmed the government is determined to stay "well within the fiscal rules" inherited from Sir Keir Starmer and his chancellor Rachel Reeves.

But Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance contributions.

He also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only has a small margin of error to do this , and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities such as such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was Defence Secretary under Keir Starmer, but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments - saying he was "certain" that Britain should lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

Questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

Reeves left a £22bn buffer in her last budget, but persistent inflation due to the Iran war could have eroded it.

On Friday, the PM said he would give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his efforts to move power out of London.

Reeves had previously said that regional mayors could be given control of some tax revenue to spend on their local priorities.

Labour pledged to devolve more powers to local councils and mayors as part of its 2024 election manifesto, in areas such as housing and transport.

More details of Burnham's plan are expected to be announced in the Budget, but the government said the rate of income tax will not change as a direct result of the reforms.

AJ Bell public policy director Tom Selby said Healey "doesn't have the luxury of pointing the finger of blame at the last administration".

"Healey will likely spend a chunk of his time leafing through the thesaurus looking for new ways to rephrase the 'tough choices' message of his predecessor," he said.

Shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the announcement of the budget date meant "89 more days of unfunded spending commitments and damaging tax speculation until we get some details".

"89 more days for Brits to wait before they know how much their taxes are going to go up to fund Burnham's spending addiction", he said.

articles.content:
If professional athletes can represent more than one country, let alone multiple clubs, why shouldn’t fans change teams?

“I was fanatically pro-German when the Germans were here to protect us against the Americans, and now that Americans are here to protect us against the Germans, I am fanatically pro-American … you and your country will have no more loyal partisan in Italy than me – but only as long as you remain in Italy.”

This passage from Joseph Heller’s Catch-22 – as an old Italian man explains the logic behind his fickle wartime expedience to a naive American soldier – plays with the question of what constitutes true strength. Universally perceived as weak, Italy are in fact the strongest nation in the second world war, according to the old man. And that, sort of, explains my feelings on football fandom.

My dad was passionate about cricket and chess. But I was a football-mad kid, and he dutifully escorted my brother and I to watch West Ham v Nottingham Forest at Upton Park in November 1987. Dad naturally knew about Brian Clough and correctly predicted it would be an entertaining game: the hosts won 3-2.

After that ridiculously exciting day as a 10-year-old, and despite living in south London, I became a Forest supporter, despite photos existing of me in Everton and Tottenham kits earlier in childhood. My mid-1980s decision to support Everton, for clarity, had been pure, unadulterated glory-hunting . Why I then decided to switch to Tottenham, I don’t recall, but it may have had something to do with Paul Gascoigne’s unique ability.

Geographically I should have supported Crystal Palace or Millwall given I was brought up between their grounds: I vividly remember visiting the Den with a Swindon-supporting schoolmate during the era of Terry Hurlock.

As a cricket fan, I have stuck with Middlesex since childhood, but there was never any familial impetus to support a football club. My brother became an Arsenal fan and when I was old enough to regularly attend games alone I started following Forest around London, including a draw at the Den in 1993-94 marred by post-match violence after a Stan Collymore equaliser ended Millwall’s playoff hopes.

When Forest sank into the doldrums after the magical mid-90s, I started to pay less attention to them in classic fairweather-fan fashion. Recently, when living in Somerset, I dabbled with being a Yeovil supporter. Now back living in London I am a regular patron at the Den and have begun to follow Millwall’s results more than Forest’s.

It’s not unusual to support an overseas club either, and after a formative experience watching Napoli lose to Chelsea in 2012 a passion for the Italian club emerged. I’ve visited Naples several times, made good friends there and seen a few games. The most memorable trip was in May 2023 when the Serie A title was sealed under Luciano Spalletti . I didn’t have a ticket but ultimately didn’t need one: the entire city was electrified by their (our) third scudetto .

For some people switching, or even mixing, football allegiances remains taboo. Devoted supporters of a single club may regard my experience as a sign of weakness, or at least exceptional fickleness. But “fan” is short for “fanatic”, and I am no longer convinced so much emotional energy should be invested in supporting any club. Why, after all, would I associate my happiness and sense of fulfilment with something I can’t control? Was the obvious and sustained misery of Arsenal fans as they edged nervously to the Premier League title worth the payoff? Perhaps it was, but there is clearly something unhealthy in that level of obsession.

It is possible, after all, to be too emotionally invested in a certain outcome for your own wellbeing. As an avid teenage follower of Forest, I felt my personal fortunes were linked to the club’s. I regarded one particularly inept late-90s defeat by Wimbledon as a personal tragedy that raised serious questions about my future happiness. I still love football – I am just more ambivalent to its outcomes.

Not only is it acceptable to switch allegiance, it actually makes more sense to base your support on what’s going on in your life at the time. If professional athletes can represent more than one country, let alone several clubs, why shouldn’t fans switch teams?

The disparity between mercenary players and loyal fans grows ever bigger and more grotesque. The players earn obscene amounts of money, and wield a disproportionate amount of power, but often show zero loyalty to a club and its fans when a better offer appears. How can any of this make sense for the lifelong supporter?

And being a diehard fan can be a compromising position in so many ways, frequently leading to defending the indefensible, from unethical petro-state sportwashing and financial doping to obvious on-field foul play and even spying. If you are a glory-hunting Manchester City devotee with a hidden Manchester United-supporting past, or have ever done a football-supporting switcheroo of any kind, do not be ashamed. There is help available. There are people who understand.

Since becoming a regular attendee at Millwall, I’ve enjoyed watching matches with one of my oldest friends and his son. A tight, noisy, old-fashioned ground, no video assistant referee, close to home … have I finally become a real fan?

As long as I live in London I will enjoy following Millwall … with Forest and Napoli thrown in. Not forgetting Dulwich Hamlet. Should I ever return to Somerset, though, I’ll be Yeovil till I die.

articles.content:
Get your balls, pucks, Scrabble boards and packs of cards away from me – all I want is space to be together, ideally with a coffee or a glass of wine

T he other day, I met a friend at the park for a catch-up. After 45 minutes of blissful note-swapping – my new tabi shoes , his new boyfriend – he pulled out a pair of ping-pong paddles and indicated a nearby table. “Fancy a quick game?” We are no longer speaking.

I’m joking, but only sort of. As far as I’m concerned, games of any sort ought to be illegal once everyone present is over the age of 12. I will make grudging exceptions for professional athletes, because apparently they’re earning a living, and realistically there is very little chance of me being asked to join in with, say, the Wimbledon final. But when it comes to anything less formal, the risk of being corralled is just too high: bat those balls, pucks, packs of cards, spinning bottles and Scrabble boards away from me, please.

Truly, there is no social situation made better by adding a game. In a setting with people I know and love, it feels like a cruel and unusual punishment to have organic conversation curtailed by something ghastly like Articulate! And although structured activities are often wheeled out for groups of strangers, that’s even worse – because now not only am I playing a game, but doing so with a bunch of people I don’t know, and I want to die.

Let’s go round the office and introduce ourselves with two truths and a lie! Let’s get each of the hens to write down their favourite thing about Milly and she can guess who wrote what! Let’s stick pins in our eyes!

In axing games, I’m not advocating for anything to replace them. On the contrary, all I want is space to be together, ideally while clutching either a coffee or a glass of wine, depending on the time of day. Don’t start thinking that activities that bridge that divide – pub quizzes, for instance – are an exception to my furious veto, either; they’re actually the most dire of all, the Uncanny Valley of organised fun. All the cues – friends, booze – are there for a lovely time, then suddenly, shhhhhh! , it’s the music round and Ollie takes this one very seriously.

Speaking of which, I’m fully aware that there exists a whole cohort who feel just as strongly as I, only in the opposite direction. I have encountered them in the wild – frothing at the mouth as they chastise you for putting your card on the left instead of the right or whatever – and frankly, they frighten me. Maybe I envy their strength of feeling. I’m not sure I’ve ever felt that righteous about anything, but it looks energising.

Am I pathologically uncompetitive? Has my lack of interest in games birthed a unique ineptitude at almost every single one? Yes and yes! Nonetheless, my years on the sidelines have made one thing abundantly clear: the real fun begins as soon as the games stop. As I said to my friend at the park: put the paddles down and get me a glass of pinot, please.

articles.title: No apologies, no freebies: the man who makes Andy Burnham’s jackets on how to weather a storm
articles.summary: Private White VC’s James Eden says PM should not be criticised for wearing a high-quality British-made brand It has not yet been two weeks since James Eden, the founder of the Manchester men’s clothier Private White VC, saw one of his best-known customers move in to No 10 Downing Street. In any sane world the man who makes the prime minister’s jackets would be popping open the champagne. His garments have been seen by millions of people and described by journalists all over the world writing about Burnham’s buttoned-down style. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Private White VC’s James Eden says PM should not be criticised for wearing a high-quality British-made brand

It has not yet been two weeks since James Eden, the founder of the Manchester men’s clothier Private White VC, saw one of his best-known customers move in to No 10 Downing Street.

In any sane world the man who makes the prime minister’s jackets would be popping open the champagne. His garments have been seen by millions of people and described by journalists all over the world writing about Burnham’s buttoned-down style.

Instead, Eden, a proud advocate of British manufacturing, has found himself defending his company in the face of a media onslaught.

“‘Man of the people’ Andy Burnham’s down-to-earth outfits are all actually designer – including an £80 T-shirt … that’s more than he cut electricity bills by,” said the Daily Mail in a front-page story.

A slew of online hate followed, with commentators accusing the PM of being a hypocrite for wearing expensive clothes when voters’ personal finances are stretched.

Eden’s clothes are not cheap, a fact he is proud of. And, perhaps typically for a man whose company was founded by his Victoria Cross-winning great-grandfather Jack, he is not going to take the “outrageous” criticism lying down.

“There should be no cynicism or criticism about a British PM promoting British goods,” he says. “There’s nothing to debate. He is the premier spokesperson of British trade and industry. Of course he should be wearing British-made stuff.”

Eden is speaking to the Guardian from the 173-year-old Manchester mill where every piece of the brand’s clothing is designed, cut and stitched together. He describes Burnham as “down-to-earth” and a “proud Mancunian”, saying the PM first started buying from the brand about three years ago.

Burnham’s dress sense is just one of many points of difference between “the king in the north” and his stuffier predecessor, Kier Starmer. The former Manchester mayor’s look is rooted in the casual style of north-west England.

It is here that Eden, a former venture capitalist, runs the clothing manufacturing business his great-grandfather established in the 1940s.

While Jack White’s company focused on raincoats, Eden’s label includes ready-to-wear alongside bespoke tailoring. Employing about 100 people, 90% of its products are made in the mill that overlooks the River Irwell, while the other 10% come from small independent suppliers, including cashmere from Scotland.

Such a focus on handcrafted items made by local craftspeople comes with a high price tag. Burnham’s waterproof Harrington jacket costs £695, his ‘ “marine” jeans £295 and a zipped polo shirt £195.

Eden does not shy away from these prices. In fact, as one of the last survivors of Britain’s once-thriving manufacturing industry, he is keen to talk about numbers.

“I don’t believe we are expensive at all,” he says. “We offer a world-class product. We don’t compromise on quality. We work with the best of the best, including the best weavers and the best finishers.” On average, Eden pays his workers £20 per hour, “not the €2 you’d get in a factory in eastern Europe or 20 pence in the far east”. His longest-serving employee has been working for the family’s companies nearly 60 years.

Due to the widespread impact of fast fashion, super-low prices and a throwaway culture around clothing have become normalised, especially in the UK.

“I understand there is an affordability issue with many of the items we sell,” he says. “[But] if you spend £10 or even £50 on a piece of clothing and it collapses after one wash, that suddenly becomes a very expensive piece of clothing,” he says.

On Instagram, Eden has posted videos where he breaks down where a customer’s money goes when they buy an item from the brand. He estimates that 99% of an £850 jacket stays in the UK economy.

“Sourcing things from local suppliers and employing people locally, all those proceeds stay within the local community and within the UK,” he says. The person who maintains the mill’s boiler started as an apprentice in the 1980s, his full-time customer service team all live locally, and every photographer, stylist and makeup artist for its shoots is Manchester-based.

It is bright news in an industry that over the past decade has found itself in a fight for survival. According to the British Retail Consortium there have been more than 400,000 retail jobs lost since 2016 while several British brands have closed or been sold off.

While Burnham has been quick to cut business rates for the hospitality industry , Eden says an easy win for the fashion industry is to allocate a proportion of defence and NHS apparel-making to UK manufacturers, the bulk of which are made in Bangladesh and China.

During the pandemic, Eden’s factory was awarded a PPE contract. He hired dozens of extra staff to make millions of medical-grade gowns and face masks. He has since repurposed the specialist equipment to make jersey collections, meaning he was able to retain many of those extra workers.

“If the Ministry of Defence or the NHS were to establish a supply chain here, the country could employ thousands of people,” he says. “At face value, the prices might not be cheaper than abroad, but that money and tax will stay in the towns where the factories are.”

Eden says he is aware of some factories in the UK paying workers cash in hand and treating them unfairly. By contrast he compares his factory to “an open kitchen” where anyone is welcome to have a tour. Photos of Burnham doing just that sparked debate in the brand’s comment section, leading Eden to write on LinkedIn: “I knew posting about Andy Burnham was going to divide the city, the country.”

Eden says he “remains apolitical”, stressing that he will support anyone who advocates for British-made products and local businesses.

David Beckham and Liam Gallagher have also visited the mill, while other high-profile customers include Eddie Redmayne, Tom Hardy, Pierce Brosnan, the Eagles, Daniel Craig and Robert De Niro. The brand has never given anything to anyone for free.

He suspects Burnham originally discovered the brand via word of mouth. “Our customers are incredibly loyal,” he says. “They wear our pieces because they absolutely love them. And then they end up talking to others about the story behind those pieces.”

Eden has found that praise from the men that buy his clothing has much more impact than a paid influencer ever could. And his rule about no complimentary pieces applies even to the prime minister. “We wouldn’t consider anyone that is after a freebie,” says Eden. “It shows that they are not respecting the time, the labour, the tradition and all the hard bloody work that’s gone into what we do. They are not for us.”

articles.content:
Brazil legend’s decision to play in Serie C at 46 has divided fans – but the man who arranged the deal has high hopes

O n a scorching summer afternoon in Ravenna, a city far better known for its fifth-century Byzantine mosaics and Dante’s tomb than for footballing glory, eyes are peeled in the historic centre for one of world football’s most recognisable figures – a man who featured in the World Cup final half-time show alongside Madonna and Ronaldo: Ronaldo de Assis Moreira, better known as Ronaldinho .

“We haven’t seen him yet,” four Ravenna supporters sitting at a cafe say with dry irony as they flip through La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy’s famous pink sports daily. They are undeniably sceptical, viewing the signing as a purely commercial operation, yet deep down they still harbour the dream of seeing the 2005 Ballon d’Or and 2002 World Cup winner wear their yellow and red shirt.

It is a small, surreal glimpse into the whirlwind that has engulfed this quiet corner of Emilia-Romagna, thanks to the business instinct of Ignazio Cipriani. Heir to the Venetian hospitality dynasty behind the renowned Harry’s Bar, Cipriani took over the club in 2024 when they were in Serie D, the fourth tier of Italian football. A native of Ravenna, he is the grandson of Raul Gardini, the Italian chemicals tycoon and sailor who steered Il Moro di Venezia to the 1992 America’s Cup final.

In his first year as president, Cipriani oversaw victory in the Serie D Cup and promotion to the professional ranks of Serie C. But that is merely the first step in a long ascent, he says: “It’s not a provocation. Serie A is the goal I declared from day one because I intend to reach it. And the Champions League remains the ultimate horizon we want to walk towards, step by step. I made this statement because I like working with my back against the wall: when you have no way out, you are forced to find solutions instead of excuses. I prefer to remove every alibi from the beginning.”

And this summer, Cipriani pulled off a surprise move – so surprising that anyone reading the headlines assumed it was a prank: bringing the 46-year-old Ronaldinho back as a player.

“We met through Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida,” Cipriani says, “two people who worked for over 20 years at AC Milan and had Ronaldinho as a player. The idea of involving him was a dream I cultivated as soon as I bought the club. Thanks to Lorenzo and Ariedo, we met, started talking, and a genuine friendship grew. From that relationship came many ideas for the club’s growth. And to the question everyone is asking, I am happy to answer: Ronaldinho will wear the Ravenna shirt as a player, and he will try – maybe scoring the last goal of his career with us!”

Meanwhile, a dedicated website has already put a special-edition shirt on sale featuring the “R10” logo – the Brazilian’s personal brand – which sold out within a few hours. It represents a striking collision of high-end global branding, small-town football, and brilliantly executed marketing stunt.

“If someone had told me three years ago that Ronaldinho was coming to Ravenna, I would have sent them straight to the psychiatric ward,” says Fabio laughing, a lifelong supporter. “The night the news broke, international headlines everywhere read ‘Ronaldinho to Ravenna’. It was an extraordinary operation.”

Ravenna is no footballing giant. Plagued by bankruptcies in 2001 and 2012, the club has spent decades bouncing around the lower tiers, with seven seasons in Serie B the highest point. Historically a volleyball stronghold, the football scene was accustomed to modest budgets and regional rivalries.

“Ronaldinho is a unique icon,” Cipriani says. “His way of playing made my generation fall in love with the game. We want him today to make the next generation of fans, in Italy and around the world, fall in love with Ravenna . It’s not just a visibility stunt; it’s about building a bridge between different eras of football and growing a truly global fanbase around it.”

To support this ambitious sporting and industrial project, the club is working with the municipality to renovate the Stadio Bruno Benelli, increasing its capacity beyond 6,300. But the president’s ultimate dream is a new multi-purpose venue open seven days a week, featuring retail spaces, concert facilities, and an integrated Hotel Cipriani linked to the city’s international tourism expansion.

For Ravenna’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, the arrival of a world-famous figure fits neatly into a broader strategy to promote the city globally. In recent years, Ravenna has been expanding its international reach beyond traditional beach tourism and commercial ports. The city is enjoying renewed ties with the Anglo-Saxon world, highlighted by a recent visit from the British royal family and the opening of the Lord Byron Museum.

“Ronaldinho brings a whole new level of global fame,” Barattoni says. “When the news broke, my phone exploded with messages from former schoolmates. For younger kids today, he might be someone to discover on YouTube, but the fascination remains intact.” With a smile, the mayor adds that, schedule permitting, he would be delighted to personally guide Ronaldinho on a tour of the city’s cultural heritage.

However, Barattoni is quick to clarify the institution’s role: “Our common ground with the club is internationalisation: bringing Ravenna’s image to the world. Ronaldinho has been a global ambassador for countless brands. There is an overarching project that can bring great visibility to the team and allow the city to showcase its initiatives beyond standard routes.” He adds: “Even before Ronaldinho’s arrival, the club did a fantastic job engaging younger generations. The average age in the stands is lower, more vibrant, and more engaged than ever before. A genuine sense of community is forming.”

Yet, fears of a hyper-commercialised image linger among traditional supporters. In the Curva Mero, such marketing moves are approached with caution. “There is a certain reluctance among some factions,” Fabio admits. “Modern football pushes values that many don’t share: rising ticket prices, losing accessibility for lower-income families. As a result, visibility and marketing stunts risk being viewed sideways.”

Cipriani demonstrates an acute awareness of these dynamics: “Without roots, no global project makes sense,” the president says. “Ravenna is not a brand we are building from scratch; it’s a history and an identity that existed before us. Tradition isn’t a brake on ambition: it’s the foundation. A club without its people is worth nothing.”

“I’m 50 years old and I’ve been coming to the stadium since my school days,” says Giovanni, another fan. “I’m rediscovering the enthusiasm of the past. If it takes an icon like Ronaldinho and a local entrepreneur to make us dream of Serie A, then so be it. The important thing is never to forget the people in the stands.”

Riding the wave of the “Ronaldinho Effect”, the season-ticket campaign has just launched with a target of selling 2,800. Ticket prices have risen by an average of about 12%, with variations across different stadium sections.

For now, Ravenna is soaking up a dizzying, galvanising atmosphere. On the pitch, the club is assembling a squad to win the league; off it, the city awaits 20 August, when Ronaldinho is expected to appear during a three-day summer festival in nearby Marina di Ravenna, organised in signature Cipriani style.

articles.title: Should you take the plunge? How to tell how clean the sea is
articles.summary: From beach ratings to apps and flags, we take a look at how swimmers can check water quality.
articles.content:
There are a variety of ways swimmers make a choice over whether to take a dip in the sea

With sewage spills and bathing water quality often in the headlines, more people are asking how clean the water is before taking a dip. From beach ratings, to apps and flags, there are now more ways than ever before to check water quality.

Bathing water quality can be affected by several factors including sewage spills, heavy rain, agricultural run-off, urban pollution and wildlife.

All of these factors can affect levels of bacteria in the water and the potential risk to swimmers.

A sewage spill does not automatically mean water quality has been affected and the absence of an alert does not guarantee clean water.

More than a third of England's designated bathing waters are in Devon and Cornwall.

This includes popular beaches such as Sennen Cove and Porthcurno on Cornwall's dramatic west coast, to Fistral on the county's north coast, Bigbury-on-Sea in south Devon and surfing hotspot Croyde Bay in north Devon.

The Environment Agency, the regulator which monitors water quality at bathing waters, rates bathing waters from "excellent" to "poor" based on bacteria found in water samples collected over a rolling four-year period.

Samples taken from the water are tested in a lab for elevated levels of E. Coli and intestinal enterococci.

The bacteria can be found in sewage and other waste and can lead to sickness, stomach cramps, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Campaigners have called for more action to be taken to stop sewage spills in south-west England

The Environment Agency says the testing regime helps "build a detailed, accurate long-term profile of a site to inform the public's decision of where to visit".

However, the testing only takes place during the bathing water season, which runs from 15 May until the end of September, and only at sites that have been already designated as bathing waters.

Critics such as Cornwall-based campaign group Surfers Against Sewage argue the system is "not fit for purpose" as people use beaches all year round.

Spills from storm overflows can impact water quality, with information on when they are discharging available online

Surfers Against Sewage (SAS) has developed their own app , external developed an app to provide alerts when bathing water quality could be affected by pollution, including sewage spills.

It says the information comes from various sources including voluntarily data from water companies in England and Wales, from sensors that monitor when a Combined Sewer Overflow operates.

It says UK water companies keep pollution alerts active for varying periods so "for the safety of water users, SAS follows the precautionary approach to keep the current alerting system in place at 48 hours".

The app also includes features such as tide information, health reporting and a live map showing active overflow discharges.

Water companies also provide information on when bathing water quality could be affected by sewage spills.

South West Water has WaterFit Live , external , which the company says helps "people make informed decisions before they swim".

An alert is displayed for 12hours and 30 minutes after a spill concludes.

A separate storm overflow map shows storm overflows in "near real time", with overflows remaining visible for 24 hours after they end.

The utility company says its storm overflow map "simply reports whether an overflow is operating and does not assess bathing water quality risk, which is assessed separately at beach level using the methodology published on the WaterFit Live website".

To get Blue Flag status a beach must get an "excellent" bathing water rating from the Environment Agency

The Blue Flag scheme , external assesses beaches against strict criteria covering water quality, environmental management, safety, accessibility and environmental education.

It is operated globally by the Foundation for Environmental Education but managed in England by Keep Britain Tidy.

Some of the Blue Flag beaches include Carbis Bay, Summerleaze and Polzeath in Cornwall, as well as Exmouth, Sidmouth and Blackpool Sands in Devon.

To get a Blue Flag, a beach must have "excellent" bathing water quality, as rated by the Environment Agency.

Unrelated to the Blue Flag scheme, red flags can sometimes be flown at beaches and bathing waters following a short-term pollution incident.

They warn people not to swim until water quality is deemed safe again.

The Environment Agency takes samples for testing at more than 150 designated bathing waters across Devon and Cornwall

A growing number of community groups across the South West are testing pollution levels at beaches, rivers and waterways.

Friends of the River Teign , external is one such group uses volunteers equipped with real-time testing kits to provide "more frequent, more localised water quality information across River Teign estuary and surrounding coastal waters".

Carolyn Sargentson said the testing would provide "a publicly accessible data set" as part of their campaign for "cleaner water".

A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the government had "taken swift action against water companies who are failing to perform" which included a ban on unfair bonuses for water bosses and making it unlawful to cover up illegal spills.

They said the government was also bringing in a new regulator, no-notice inspections and "MOT-style" checks on water firms.

Bathing water regulations were being upgraded "for the first time in over a decade", they added.

Follow BBC Devon on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk , external .

England sewage spills nearly halved in 2025 due mostly to drier weather

articles.content:
Animated cats banter tediously in a show that’s determined to shock, but which leaves you checking your watch to see how long is left. It’s lazy, dated and far too pleased with itself

A ccording to multiverse theory, there are parallel realities in which news of a new Ricky Gervais project instils a feeling other than dread. But we don’t live in them. Having seen his new series, Alley Cats (Netflix, from Friday 7 August), a boorish banter-vehicle in which animated cats shoot the breeze like a bunch of pub bores, I’m not sure what there is to report – other than the fact that I didn’t laugh once. Considering what a fan I once was, I find this remarkable. What happened?

Woke happened, is what his diehard fans would say. Gervais has paid the price of a shifting Overton window on jokes about dwarves and disabled people and trans people. You can’t say anything any more, they lament, while defending a wealthy, highly platformed man who proves the opposite. They’re not wrong, though – politics plays a part. While writing this, I stepped outside to say hello to a queer friend who was, naturally, buying a bicycle in the street. I asked her what she made of Ricky Gervais.

“He’s defunct. We don’t need him any more,” she said, as if describing DVDs by post. His work didn’t make her laugh now, she said, but added that this was a relief. If he was both problematic and she found him funny, she’d have to suffer a contradiction within herself. He’d let her off the hook; but a comedian’s politics and their craft are still different things.

I like contradictions and dislike safe comedy. I actually agree that swathes of our culture are risk-averse and boring. Nothing makes me laugh harder than a good transgressive joke. Humour is often about dissolving dogma, acting as a safety valve for our collective id. The darker meats, close to the bone, have the juiciest flavour. But “good” is as important as “transgressive”. Alley Cats leans on one at the expense of the other. That’s why it limps.

The series follows a gang of stray cats, who mostly spend their time watching TV on a sofa in a derelict house. Gus, voiced by Ricky Gervais, is a fat ginger tom, who bellows ignorant or misanthropic opinions over everyone else. Ponce, voiced by Tom Basden , is a pampered, middle-class pedigree who talks sense but is fatally undermined because he has no balls, lol. Then there’s Puke ( David Earl ), a mangy pervert with a penchant for inter-species sex who says things such as “I gave a hedgehog anal once”.

articles.title: Football Australia and AFC welcome Fifa climbdown on World Cup sell-off plan
articles.summary: FA says some principles of the game ‘should never change’ AFC calls for ‘proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect’ Football Australia and the Asian Football Confederation have welcomed Fifa’s climbdown over its failed plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors, with FA chair Anter Isaac saying some principles of football “should never change”. Fifa president Gianni Infantino on Saturday confirmed the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal had been scrapped following widespread backlash led by Uefa, which asserted its member nations would boycott all Fifa tournaments unless the plan was withdrawn. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Football Australia and the Asian Football Confederation have welcomed Fifa’s climbdown over its failed plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors, with FA chair Anter Isaac saying some principles of football “should never change”.

Fifa president Gianni Infantino on Saturday confirmed the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal had been scrapped following widespread backlash led by Uefa, which asserted its member nations would boycott all Fifa tournaments unless the plan was withdrawn.

FA had resisted immediate criticism of the proposal, asking instead for more information to digest and “properly assess” the implications as part of a consultation process before it formed an official position.

The Asian Football Confederation, of which Australia is a part, had stopped short of threatening a boycott but issued a strongly worded statement that echoed Uefa’s concerns. Concacaf, which is responsible for North and Central America and the Caribbean, also strongly opposed the sell-off.

In a statement on Saturday, Isaac acknowledged that football should never stand still but certain principles of the game should not be tampered with.

“The discussions of recent days have reinforced an important principle of good governance: proposals of global significance should be developed through robust consultation, appropriate governance processes and meaningful engagement with member associations before they are presented for consideration,” Isaac said.

“Football has never stood still, nor should it. Some principles, however, should never change. Integrity. Independence. Good governance. Transparency. Meaningful consultation. Due process.

“These are not constraints on progress. They are what make lasting progress possible. Ultimately, the strength of football’s institutions depends on the confidence and trust of the global football family. That trust is earned not simply through good decisions, but through the integrity of the processes that lead to them.

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al-Khalifa also welcomed Fifa’s decision to stand down from its plans, which aimed to raise up to $4.2bn by selling about a 20% stake to private investors in the newly created FFE, which would run the World Cup and other Fifa events.

Salman said he expected “any initiative that ‌has the potential to impact global football will be presented and discussed with the confederations, the Fifa ​Council, member associations and other stakeholders in a timely, transparent and meaningful manner”.

“The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established ⁠governance structures of our game,” he added in a letter posted on the AFC’s website.

The AFC represents 47 member nations, including Australia, along with the likes of China, Japan and Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Tim Dowling: can I conquer my wife’s book club? I can certainly divide it
articles.summary: She says I’m not allowed to select books as I’m the only man and not a full member. But how could they not love Death Comes for the Archbishop? My wife would have everyone in our book club believe that the First Rule of Book Club is: Tim Is Never Allowed to Pick the Book. Having failed in her several attempts to have me removed from book club , she has settled for imposing restrictions on my participation to make my membership seem second tier. “You’re not allowed to pick because you’re not really even in book club,” she says to me before every meeting. “You’re like a mascot.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
She says I’m not allowed to select books as I’m the only man and not a full member. But how could they not love Death Comes for the Archbishop?

M y wife would have everyone in our book club believe that the First Rule of Book Club is: Tim Is Never Allowed to Pick the Book. Having failed in her several attempts to have me removed from book club , she has settled for imposing restrictions on my participation to make my membership seem second tier.

“You’re not allowed to pick because you’re not really even in book club,” she says to me before every meeting. “You’re like a mascot.”

“What are you talking about?” I always say. “I’m the beating heart of book club.”

In truth, there is no First Rule of Book Club. There is, however, a longstanding protocol under which my suggestions are given less weight than anyone else’s. This is partly because I’m the only man and my opinions sometimes go against the grain of majority taste, and partly because the only time I did get to pick the book everyone loathed it, including me.

But more than a year has passed since then, and on a night when my wife and I are hosting book club in our kitchen, I feel ready to try again.

Last year I started keeping a list of the books I’ve read on my phone, because I could never remember the names of any of them, even the most recent ones. This list is where I went for inspiration when I needed a solid, unassailable choice.

“What about a classic?” I say casually, when the time to choose arrives toward the close of the evening. Tonight’s book has been universally popular, and everyone is in a mood to see the point of book club.

The book I have in mind – from midway through my list – is indeed a classic, a century old and a recognised masterpiece, but also obscure enough that I can be fairly certain no one else has read it. My oldest son recommended it to me, and I in turn recommended it to his brother. We were all in agreement: a banger.

“ Death Comes for the Archbishop ?” says Emma, with transparent scepticism.

Three weeks later I wake early in the morning to find my wife staring at me over the top of her Kindle as if I have done something terrible. Searching my memory for recent crimes, I find myself blameless. But she is still staring.

“Stupid priests riding around on donkeys everywhere,” she says. “Is it like this all the way through?”

Two afternoons later, while I’m sitting in my office shed, I develop an eerie sense that somewhere nearby I am being discussed. I cross the garden to find my wife talking to the middle one in the kitchen.

“Whatever it’s called,” she is saying. “Death Comes for the Fucking Archbishop.”

“Banger is maybe not the word I would choose,” he says. “It’s quite slow, and not much happens.”

The following Thursday we arrive at Emma’s house for the next instalment of book club. Often the early part of the evening is taken up with preliminary topics: local gossip, domestic mishaps, recent holidays. Not this time.

My wife raises her objection to the many journeys by donkey. Suzy, with a cry of affection, lists all the donkeys by name.

The discussion becomes animated. Death Comes for the Archbishop has split book club opinion down the middle. But as certain key episodes are recounted in detail, I fall silent. Fran turns to me and suggests that, given the intensity of feeling, I might care to defend my choice.

“I can’t,” I say. “I don’t remember anything. I read it, like, a year and a half ago.”

“Why would I?” I say. “The whole point of being the chooser is so you get a freebie.”

“You see?” my wife says. “This is why he’s never allowed to pick the book.”

articles.title: Blind date: ‘I joked we should join the young people for a club night. We didn’t’
articles.summary: Richard, 63, a communications consultant, meets Katrina, 60, a GP What were you hoping for? Easy conversation with someone interesting, smart and relaxed. Continue reading...
articles.content:
What were you hoping for? Easy conversation with someone interesting, smart and relaxed.

First impressions? Katrina arrived and my blind date trepidation vanished. She looked good, was warm, and the conversation flowed straight away.

What did you talk about? Our grownup kids. Running. Travel. Our devotion to our coffee machines.

Most awkward moment? I thought Katrina was still working her way through her post-meal mint tea, so was taken aback when she said, “Shall we call it a night?”

Would you introduce Katrina to your friends? Yes. I’m sure she gets on really well with most people.

Blind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the UK) and online at theguardian.com every Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you can read all about how we put it together here . What questions will I be asked? We ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.

Can I choose who I match with? No, it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely to be.

Can I pick the photograph? No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.

How should I answer? Honestly but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.

Will I see the other person’s answers? No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.

Can I do it in my home town? Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.

What do you think Katrina made of you? She laughed at a few things I said, and we had quite a few things in common, so I think she felt I was easy company.

Did you go on somewhere? As we left the restaurant and saw a queue of young people outside a bar, I joked that we should join them for a club night. We didn’t.

If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be? Nothing. I had a fun evening with a lovely woman and don’t think it could have been improved.

Would you meet again? I really enjoyed Katrina’s company, we talked and laughed a lot. So of course.

What did you talk about? Coffee snobbery – our coffee machines (identical), the best beans, our children aspiring to own the same machine.

Good table manners? Impeccable. Attentive without ever being overbearing.

What do you think Richard made of you? I hope he saw me as warm, approachable and engaging.

Did you go on somewhere? No. We looked at the club opposite, but agreed that wasn’t going to happen.

If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be? Honestly, not much. I really enjoyed the evening, and for a blind date it exceeded my expectations.

Would you meet again? Possibly, as friends – I’m not sure there was a romantic spark, but I really enjoyed his company. I’d happily introduce him to the joys of the hill at Ashton Court parkrun.

Katrina and Richard ate at Marmo in Bristol . Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com

articles.title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for oyster mushroom burgers with five-spice cabbage | Meera Sodha recipes
articles.summary: These roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressing Not every plant makes a great burger filling. You might think pulses or potatoes for heft, but the lack of texture and propensity to mush can be unsatisfying. This is where mushrooms excel; they trade in satisfaction. Roasting them brings out their natural umami and removes water content, leaving them chewy, caramelised and occasionally crisp. They can also make friends with the most unlikely of ingredients, like they have here with peanut butter, soy, agave and sesame. Continue reading...

These roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressing

N ot every plant makes a great burger filling. You might think pulses or potatoes for heft, but the lack of texture and propensity to mush can be unsatisfying. This is where mushrooms excel; they trade in satisfaction. Roasting them brings out their natural umami and removes water content, leaving them chewy, caramelised and occasionally crisp. They can also make friends with the most unlikely of ingredients, like they have here with peanut butter, soy, agave and sesame.

Now, two types of agave syrup are available in the supermarkets: dark is richer, more caramelly; lighter is simpler and more neutral. If you only have or can find light, use that. These mushrooms can be cooked on skewers on a barbecue, but do so over indirect heat under a watchful eye.

For the mushrooms 600g oyster mushrooms 60g smooth peanut butter 2 tbsp toasted sesame oil 1 tbsp dark agave syrup 2 tbsp red or brown miso 1½ tbsp light soy sauce 1 tbsp apple cider vinegar 3 garlic cloves , peeled and minced

For the five-spice cabbage 200g white cabbage , finely shredded 5 spring onions , trimmed, greens and whites finely shredded ½ tsp fine sea salt ½ tsp ground five-spice 1½ tbsp apple cider vinegar 15g coriander leaves , finely chopped 1 tbsp mayonnaise , plus extra to serve 4 brioche burger buns , to serve

Heat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9, and line two trays with baking paper.

If your mushrooms are in big clumps, break them gently into individual mushrooms and put them in a large bowl. Put the peanut butter, sesame oil, agave, miso, soy sauce, vinegar and garlic in a small bowl, stir until you have a smooth sauce, then pour this over the mushrooms.

Using your hands like claws in an arcade machine, carefully toss to cover all the mushrooms in the sauce. Spread the mushrooms over the two trays, then bake for 12-15 minutes, until all the liquid has dried out and the edges are charred, then remove from the oven.

While the mushrooms are cooking, make the slaw. Put the cabbage and spring onions in a big bowl, sprinkle over the salt and scrunch with (clean) hands. Mix through all the other salad ingredients.

To assemble the burgers, split and toast the brioche buns – one minute in a toaster works well. Spread one cut side of each bun with mayo, pile on a quarter of the mushrooms, then top with some slaw. Repeat with the other burgers, clap on the lids and serve.

articles.content:
The best sunscreen is the one that you’ll use everyday. We asked doctors for the best SPFs for every face, from acne-prone skin to babies and everything in between

W e all know what sunscreen is ( or do we? ) and that we should use it (right?). But you may have heard internet chatter about some sunscreen ingredients being “toxic” and wondered: how do I know if my sunscreen is safe to use ?

Understanding why something so necessary might actually be bad for you is the first step. Because sunscreen makes health claims such as preventing sunburn and reducing risk of skin cancer and premature skin aging, it is regulated for safety and effectiveness in the US by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as an over-the-counter or non-prescription drug (rather than a cosmetic).

The FDA evaluates OTC medication ingredients by the standard of “generally recognized as safe and effective” ( Grase ). “Nontoxic”, “clean” or “natural” are not legally defined terms to label sunscreen in the US. They’re essentially marketing; any brand can use them without meeting a specific standard. The key is to read the label carefully to determine active and inactive ingredients to evaluate those claims.

There are an overwhelming number of options on the market, but only three sunscreen ingredients are considered Grase : the mineral filters zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, and bemotrizinol , a chemical filter that is new to the US market.

As for what ingredients to watch out for? Parabens, which are preservatives used in many cosmetics, and phthalates, which are chemicals used to improve the texture and shelf life of sunscreen. Both are considered safe within regulatory limits, but parabens can cause skin irritation and endocrine disruption, while phthalates mimic estrogen activity and can possibly disrupt hormones, affecting fertility or child development. To avoid these ingredients, look for “paraben-free” on the label or check the inactive ingredients list and look for acronyms such as DEHP, DBP or DEP, which are different types of phthalates. (Phthalates are often listed as “fragrance” on labels, so one trick is to avoid artificial fragrances.)

We asked dermatologist experts to weigh in on what makes sunscreens safest and recommend their favorite nontoxic sunscreens.

Michael Girardi, MD, FAAD , is the vice-chair for faculty development and scientific innovation and the Evans professor of dermatology at Yale School of Medicine in New Haven, Connecticut.

Sapna Palep, MD, FAAD, MBA is a board-certified dermatologist and the founder of Spring Street Dermatology and Journelle Skin in New York City.

Divya Shokeen, MD, FAAD is a board-certified dermatologist and the founder of OSVI Dermatology and Surgery Institute in Los Angeles. She is also the founder of Oathology Skincare.

Tinted sunscreen provides sun protection with a touch of makeup coverage. It generally contains active mineral ingredients, but some can also contain chemical screens – just make sure to check the label. One disadvantage is that some brands have limited shade ranges, making it hard to find a perfect match. (If there’s SPF in your foundation, you should also wear sunscreen. The Skin Cancer Foundation recommends an SPF of 30 or higher, 50 or higher for a day outdoors, reapplying every two hours. Tinted moisturizers or foundations with SPF may not meet those standards.)

“It is one of my favorite tinted sunscreens,” says Palep. “It provides UVA and UVB protection, as well as blue light protection from screens, and contains zinc oxide and niacinamide.” Zinc oxide is a mineral sunscreen, widely considered safe; niacinamide may help reduce inflammation and improve skin elasticity .

If you’d rather eliminate all chemical sunscreens, try this untinted pick. “It contains only mineral active agents, but gives a minimal whitish hue ,” says Girardi.

For deeper skin tones, he recommends tinted mineral sunscreens such as:

Palep says: “This is great for pale skin, offering broad spectrum sun protection and antioxidant protection. The formula is lightweight and not sticky or greasy and absorbs quickly, leaving skin feeling soft and smooth.”

For little ones, Shokeen recommends using only mineral formulations : “My young kids are in the habit of wearing sunscreen every day on their face and hands.”

Girardi also opts for “zinc oxide and titanium dioxide only”. Bemotrizinol, when it’s available, is expected to be used in pediatric formulations, he says, and suggests extra sun protection in clothing and bathing suits. “Use a hat early and often to get them used to it.” This is also a great option if you’re never used sunscreen and are overwhelmed with the abundance of choices.

It contains zinc oxide, aloe vera and vegetarian glycerine and is EWG verified .

“Fully mineral sunscreen can sometimes be better for sensitive skin ,” says Shokeen. She likes this one because “it negates a lot of the red in the skin, especially if you have rosacea .”

“I recommend this for anyone with sensitive skin,” says Palep. “It’s a mineral sunscreen that uses zinc oxide to protect against the sun’s rays and has centella asiatica , which has anti-inflammatory properties .”

This is Palep’s pick for oily skin. “The formula is oil-free and non-comedogenic so it won’t clog pores, while adding hydration to skin with hyaluronic acid . It’s lightweight, doubles as a mattifying makeup primer and layers well under makeup.”

This is a budget-friendly option that makes similar claims as the more pricey Shiseido – it’s oil-free, has a matte finish, and is also fragrance-free.

“It’s my brand,” says Shokeen, “so I know that it contains azelaic acid ” – which is an ingredient that claims anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and antioxidant benefits.

While these sunscreens are convenient, most people just spray and go, says Shokeen, who doesn’t recommend them. Unless you rub in the product after you spray, you don’t get enough coverage. “I also steer patients away from spray preparations, which go on inconsistently, leaving gaps in protection,” says Girardi. “I much prefer creams and lotions. Sprays also have the added risk of inhalation.”

“The spray is powerful to evenly disperse sunscreen all over the body (you still need to rub it in though),” says Palep, “and has the classic scent the brand is known for. It smells like a vacation!” (The brand website describes the scent as “notes of coconut, banana, pool water, pool toy and swimsuit Lycra”.)

“Mineral sticks can be helpful for noses, ears and around the eyes and are easy to keep in a bag for quick reapplication,” says Girardi, who doesn’t recommend them as your only sunscreen option.

“Mineral sunscreens that use zinc oxide or titanium dioxide for sun protection are generally considered to be reef-safe ,” says Palep. She also likes the Thinksport Safe Sunscreen Stick SPF 30+ and Project Reef’s SPF 50 Sheer Mineral Sunscreen .

Girardi’s pick is designed to be water-resistant and also claims to dry clear on the skin, eliminating the possibility of any white cast.

“It would trick you into thinking it’s a moisturizer instead of a sunscreen,” says Palep.

“This is a great option for skin of color, as the brand offers a variety of shades to match a wide range of skin tones,” Palep says. “The formula is heavily pigmented and applies easily to the skin with your fingers or a makeup brush, without feeling heavy or greasy. Coverage is buildable, so it covers uneven skin tone and acne marks too. Broad spectrum SPF 50 is ideal for delicate facial skin.”

There is a sunscreen out there that’s right for you, if you know what to look for and what you want.

Chemical sunscreens such as avobenzone, oxybenzone, octinoxate and homosalate are carbon-based molecules that sink into the upper layers of skin, absorb UV radiation and then release the energy as a small amount of heat. A series of FDA-commissioned studies between 2019 and 2021 showed that these filters were absorbed into the bloodstream in detectable levels after typical application.

“Once the FDA figured out that several of the chemical agents used in sunscreen formulations exceeded a certain blood level with regular applications, the FDA required further testing to check for toxicity,” Girardi says. The FDA proposed new toxicology testing in 2019 ; however, none of the disputed ingredients will be removed from shelves while waiting for new data.

In June 2026, the FDA added bemotrizinol (BEMT) to the list of permitted active sunscreen ingredients. It is the first new active ingredient added to the OTC sunscreen safety monograph (the FDA’s official safety rules) since the late 1990s. BEMT has been marketed in Europe and many countries as a sunscreen ingredient for years. It’s broad spectrum, so it protects against both UVA and UVB rays and has low levels of skin absorption, so it’s generally considered Grase for adults and kids (six months and older). Sunscreens that contain BEMT are not as shiny as mineral sunscreens can be, Girardi says. In the US, sunscreens with BEMT should hit store shelves in September under the brand name Parsol Shield .

Look for zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, which are the two FDA-approved Grase mineral active ingredients. On the skin’s surface, they create a physical barrier that works to scatter and absorb UV rays, keeping them from penetrating the upper skin layers. Both have long safety records, but some formulations with higher concentrations can leave a white tone on the skin, which is more apparent on deeper skin hues. Sunscreen companies have addressed this by reducing the size of particles via micronization , a process that reduces the size of standard zinc oxide and titanium dioxide particles.

Nano particles are smaller than standard-sized particles of zinc oxide and titanium dioxide. This reduces the white cast some mineral sunscreens leave on the skin. Research has concluded that these nano particles don’t penetrate healthy, intact skin in significant amounts – but if your skin barrier is severely compromised, this may not apply.

A fun (and useful) souvenir from a trip abroad is sunscreen, especially from Europe and Asia, where sunscreens are treated as cosmetic products and not OTC drugs, like they are in the US. This allows for a more streamlined approval process and a broader range of UV filters. If you’re not traveling anytime soon, you can order sunscreens from specialized websites such as yesstyle.com or frenchpharmacy.com ). Popular brands include Beauty of Joseon (a Korean brand), Anessa Perfect UV Sunscreen (from Japan and La Roche-Posay Anthelios UVmune 400 from France.

Preservatives help keep our skincare products from spoiling and phthalates help with the texture and fragrance. Methylparaben, propylparaben and other parabens are preservatives used in many cosmetics and some sunscreens. The FDA currently considers parabens safe at permitted concentrations in topical products.

Phthalates are chemicals used to improve the texture of personal care products, making them feel smoother and spread easily. Like parabens, many phthalates are considered safe within regulatory limits and remain permitted in the US at regulated levels. The Environmental Working Group website calls phthalates “still widely used chemicals that pollute almost everyone’s bodies”.

The most toxic sunscreen seems to be the one that you do not use, according to our experts. “I wouldn’t consider any sunscreen that is sold in the US to be toxic, so they are all ‘nontoxic,’” Palep says. “There is more of a health risk of not wearing sunscreen and getting skin cancer, versus using a chemical sunscreen and having health issues stem from using the chemical sunscreen. Most patients are not using enough of a chemical sunscreen to cause an issue.”

“People should keep in mind that ‘nontoxic’ here is a double-edged term since UV radiation from the sun is very toxic ,” says Giraldi. “It causes mutations and is the biggest risk factor for these deadly skin cancers. And, of course, many like that using sunscreen also decreases signs of skin aging.”

Shokeen agrees. “I do skin cancer surgeries all day long,” she says. “Calling sunscreen ‘toxic’ is 100% a scare tactic – no ifs, ands or buts. So many things we put on topically get into the bloodstream, like retinols. That doesn’t mean it’s bad.” She also finds that her millennial clients are “faring the best”, she says, because they are diligent in their self-care routines (anti-aging potions, wrinkle-fighting lasers such as Fraxel and UltraClear, for example). “They are very good about using sunscreen to protect their investment.”

articles.title: Fifa scraps proposal to sell off stakes in World Cup after widespread backlash
articles.summary: Gianni ⁠Infantino issues statement on controversial plan ‘This proposal will not proceed,’ confirms Fifa president Gianni Infantino’s proposal to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors has sensationally collapsed, with the Fifa president admitting the project “has created divisions of a nature that are no longer in the interest of the objective”, amid widespread anger globally. The plan had caused ructions within football around the world, leading Uefa to threaten a boycott of future Fifa tournaments if it was not shelved. Other confederations had also come out in opposition while one of Infantino’s senior advisors, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned on Friday in protest at the scheme. The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, had also aimed a scathing rebuke at Infantino’s “serious lack of respect” in seeking to force it through with minimal consultation. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Gianni Infantino’s proposal to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors has sensationally collapsed, with the Fifa president admitting the project “has created divisions of a nature that are no longer in the interest of the objective”, amid widespread anger globally.

The plan had caused ructions within football around the world, leading Uefa to threaten a boycott of future Fifa tournaments if it was not shelved. Other confederations had also come out in opposition while one of Infantino’s senior advisors, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned on Friday in protest at the scheme. The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, had also aimed a scathing rebuke at Infantino’s “serious lack of respect” in seeking to force it through with minimal consultation.

It has led Infantino to back down amid speculation the venture capital firm Thrive Capital, which was leading the proposed investor group, had also expressed doubts after a week that threatened to tear the sport apart. Infantino’s previously secure presidency has come under severe pressure and it remains to be seen whether his climbdown will be enough to save his position.

“Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” Infantino said in a statement.

“Our purpose has always been – and will always be – to unite and improve. As a result, this proposal will not proceed. Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support.”

But the plan was roundly rejected by European countries’ FAs, who agreed upon a boycott at an emergency meeting on Thursday. Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, the latter with a stinging statement on Friday morning, had also made their distaste clear . While Infantino retains a stronghold in Africa he was left with nowhere to go, the numbers to push through the plan in any credible form having eluded him.

Attention will now turn to Infantino’s future given the scale of the internal revolt within Fifa and the severe hit his standing has taken elsewhere. It is unlikely his withdrawal of the plan will sway member associations who had already become deeply disenchanted by his handling of the Folarin Balogun affair, which unfolded three weeks previously during the World Cup. But some observers have wondered whether recourse to Fifa’s reserves, which stand at around $4bn (£2.97bn), for the promised FFE cash would convince enough federations to save his skin.

Uefa and other confederations have stepped up their search for candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term. Their appetite is unlikely to change and time will tell whether Infantino can turn his fortunes around after an episode that has had a shattering impact on his credibility.
