articles.title: Scientist's lifelong obsession with mystery of elusive 'pink zebra' seaweed
articles.summary: An ancient algae first spotted four decades ago will now join the collection of the Natural History Museum.
articles.content:
The Great Barrier Reef might be the world's most famous underwater ecosystem, but hidden in UK waters lies an ancient marine world you may not have heard of.

Known as maerl beds, these carpets of coral-like seaweed create some of the richest habitats in the sea.

And 40 years ago, while studying one such bed for her PhD, Prof Christine Maggs found a fragment of pink-striped seaweed living on maerl she had never seen before.

The discovery would become a lifelong obsession and a decades-long scientific puzzle.

Maerl beds may closely resemble corals but they are in fact thousands of pieces of free-living calcified seaweed that can interlock to create a carpet brimming with life.

Hours of trawling through the literature seemed to confirm that no-one else had known what this little seaweed that lived on maerl was either. Prof Maggs suspected it was a new species to science.

She continued the hunt after her PhD, and the tiny seaweed would accompany her throughout her career, with fleeting glimpses including once on an underwater animal called a sea squirt, although never enough material to pin its identity down.

The Natural History Museum collection of seaweed pressings which the new species has joined

But then two years ago, researchers surveying maerl beds in Cornwall found a sample, which they thought might be Prof Maggs' elusive seaweed.

Prof Maggs bought a wine fridge in anticipation, the perfect dark, cool environment to store it while tests were carried out to prove it was, indeed, a new species.

"I just kept hoping that I would find out, it's been over four decades," she said.

She has now shared the discovery exclusively with the BBC, and a sample of the species has joined the Natural History Museum's official collection.

The scientific divers who found the sample were mapping and analysing seaweeds to check on the health of Cornish maerl beds, a project organised by Natural England.

This type of diving is specialised and expensive, involving difficult logistics and a large amount of equipment. But for the researchers involved, the experience is extremely rewarding.

"It's such a privilege to go diving somewhere like this and you never get long enough. It's different every single time," Angie Gall at Natural England says.

They have seen spider crabs taking a stroll, starfish, king scallops and goby fish.

Amongst the collection of bags brought up on one such Cornish trip were cuttings of a small red algae which was pink-banded with pincer tips.

Christine Maggs in 1982 in a home-made drysuit with her PhD supervisor Mike Guiry beside her

Francis Bunker, a freelance and independent marine biologist, kept finding the tiny seaweed in samples he had collected on that survey.

"I suppose you've got to be a bit nerdy," he says, explaining he takes a magnifying glass with him diving. "You've got to be awed by it all, which I never cease to be."

He suspected the tiny seaweed might be what Prof Maggs had long been searching for. He gathered as much as he could and sent it to her in London.

Prof Maggs needed to grow the seaweed big enough to be DNA sequenced. She turned to her trusty cool chamber - the wine fridge.

"This particular seaweed is so small I needed to get some molecular data," Prof Maggs explains. "That's why this has taken me 40 years."

But the wait was worth it. With the help of Prof Beatriz de Barros Barreto, who worked on the DNA sequencing, Prof Maggs has put the pieces of the puzzle together to reveal the seaweed is indeed new to science.

"We knew that maerl was a rich, biodiverse habitat, but we didn't necessarily realise that we'd be still finding new species that live on that maerl," Prof Maggs says.

"It's great," Bunker adds. "I think it's what spurs you on really, finding a new species. It's like the icing on the cake, or the cherry on top."

Prof Maggs' findings are soon to be published in the peer-reviewed journal Phycologia.

Seaweeds are one of the most ancient forms of life - having developed more than 1bn years ago - and many provide a critical food source for fish and a haven for them to lay their eggs.

For humans, the abundant minerals and anti-inflammatory properties of certain seaweeds have seen their extracts used in medicines from treating acid reflux to wound dressings.

"We really have to look after seaweeds, we really have to love them," Prof Juliet Brodie, a leading seaweed expert, explains in the vaults of the Natural History Museum surrounded by a collection of seaweed pressings the new species is joining.

Finding a new species, although exciting in itself, plays an important role in keeping an eye on the maerl's health over time.

"They're really precious," she adds. "I've often pondered to myself, what would the world be like without seaweeds? You would be taking away your nurseries for some of your economically important fish. But you would also [remove] the immense diversity that makes our world function."

Prof Craig Schneider, professor of biology at Trinity College Connecticut, who was not involved in the study, says the discovery of the new species is "significant" to science.

He said it could also add to interest in protecting maerl beds, which were "already of the greatest importance to all of the other plants, animals and microbes in the ecological community that they support".

Maerl beds are rare in Britain. They are classed as a threatened and declining habitat under the OSPAR convention - an international agreement for environmental protection in the North-East Atlantic.

There are currently four protected maerl sites in the UK, including the Fal and Helford Special Area of Conservation (SAC).

But the less studied beds off the south Cornish coast, where the new species has also been found living on the maerl, are not formally protected.

Defra says it may not be necessary to make this area of maerl beds an SAC, "nor is there a requirement, to protect all examples of a species or habitats."

Part of the reason, it says, is balancing nature recovery with "wider priorities including offshore wind development and fisheries."

Whilst protection is debated, the researcher-divers continue their work to document and potentially recover new species, and perhaps the most exciting part, to name them.

Prof Maggs' new species will be known scientifically as ceramium ruenessianum , in honour of her colleague who has studied this type of species for the last 40 years.

As for the seaweed's common name, a firm favourite amongst the scientific divers is "pink-zebra weed".

Other ideas include "pink-banded bandit" and "ribbon claw". Prof Maggs is inviting the public to make their suggestions.

articles.title: Isaac Beacroft walks to gold on mixed day for Australia at Commonwealth Games
articles.summary: Sarah Billings claims Australia’s first 800m women’s bronze in 36 years But disappointment for three other track and field stars in Glasgow Teenage race walker Isaac Beacroft hit the accelerator on a dramatic final lap in the 10,000m then had to hit it again, celebrating Commonwealth Games gold 20 metres before the finish despite his Kenyan rival Stephen Kihu lurking just a few steps behind. The result was the Australian highlight on a mixed day at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, as Sarah Billings claimed her country’s first 800m women’s bronze in 36 years, even as track and field stars Nina Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and Lachie Kennedy were left disappointed. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Sarah Billings claims Australia’s first 800m women’s bronze in 36 years

Teenage race walker Isaac Beacroft hit the accelerator on a dramatic final lap in the 10,000m then had to hit it again, celebrating Commonwealth Games gold 20 metres before the finish despite his Kenyan rival Stephen Kihu lurking just a few steps behind.

The result was the Australian highlight on a mixed day at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, as Sarah Billings claimed her country’s first 800m women’s bronze in 36 years, even as track and field stars Nina Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and Lachie Kennedy were left disappointed.

Beacroft, the under-20 world record holder, stormed away from Kihu with 300m to go to secure gold. “Probably the last 15 laps, I was just waiting for Kihu to go, but he never did, so I sat in, and eventually had to go,” he told Channel Seven. “I went hard, about 95%, and then I knew he was going to come with me, but then I had another gear in there to really make it over.”

He secured the breakthrough win, but not without fraying the nerves of his father and coach David. “He’s having a panic,” Beacroft told Channel Seven with a smile. “He thought I was going to get chased down, and started celebrating too early. Rubbish.”

Beacroft Sr, a former race walker himself, admitted he might have done things differently. “I just saw the guy make another surge and I’m like, ‘Oh, don’t do too much too soon’, but he held him off. It was nice, it was good, really good.”

The 19-year-old, whose celebrations and interviews in Glasgow marked the birth of a new showman in Australian athletics, now heads to Oregon to compete at the world juniors in just nine days.

Billings’ historic bronze was a mix of brain and braun, as she positioned herself well with a lap to go and pushed all the way up the final straight. The Australian finished behind English winner Georgia Hunter Bell and Kenyan Lilian Odira, last year’s world champion who Billings almost beat at the line.

While that bronze medal provided unbridled joy for Billings, a silver in the pole vault for Nina Kennedy left the Paris Olympic champion with mixed emotions. “If you don’t laugh, you’ll cry,” she said. “So I’m trying to put on a happy face right now, but look, I’m disappointed. I wanted the gold.”

In blustery conditions she cleared 4.65m but finished second on a count-back to Eliza McCartney, who won New Zealand’s second track and field gold at these Games after Zoe Hobbs’s 100m success.

Lewis, who finished third behind Hobbs in that 100m final two days ago, ran gallantly to finish sixth in the final of the 200m, won by Adaejah Hodge of the British Virgin Islands. “Not what I wanted for the 200,” Lewis said. “I made the final which was one of my goals so I’m still proud of that, and I look towards the relay.”

In the men’s 200m, Lachie Kennedy also finished sixth. The 100m silver medallist and new 9.85sec man started well but faded behind South African winner Sinesipho Dambile. “I knew if I wanted to win, I was going to have to risk it,” Kennedy said. “Look, I gave it a red hot crack. Didn’t have enough juice in the tank. Credit to the winners. But yeah, I’m gassed.”

Like Lewis, Lachie Kennedy will compete in the 4x100m relay on a busy final day of competition in Glasgow, which also includes men’s and women’s mile races. The women’s event is a chance for Jessica Hull to get one back on Claudia Hollingsworth, who caused the Paris silver medallist to fall in a controversial 1500m final at the national championships in April .

The men’s event promises to one of the races of these games. It will feature Scottish pair Jake Wightman and Josh Kerr, who broke the men’s world record in the mile last month, as well as reigning Commonwealth champion Olli Hoare and his fellow Australians Adam Spencer and Cam Myers. The latter was described by Wightman this week as “the future of the sport” .

articles.title: Infantino under huge pressure after plan for World Cup sell-off sparks resignation and rebuke

Infantino is under huge pressure after his plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors met a tide of opposition from around the globe. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The walls started closing in on Gianni Infantino after another dramatic day that saw one of his senior advisers resign and brought a scathing rebuke from Fifa’s own chief operating officer.

Infantino is under huge pressure after his plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors met a tide of opposition from around the globe. European countries have already promised to boycott Fifa competitions if he does not shelve the scheme but Friday’s developments, which led to two key members of his inner circle distancing themselves from him, may prove equally damaging to any prospects of salvaging his presidency.

Meanwhile Uefa and other confederations are actively seeking candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term. The pressure that has built since this week’s revelations casts doubt on whether the previously unassailable Swiss, who has doubled down on the proposals, will be able to cling on for that long.

The resignation of Carlos Cordeiro, one of Infantino’s senior advisers since 2021, struck a fresh blow upon Infantino hours after Uefa’s 55 members had unanimously threatened a boycott. Cordeiro, a former US Soccer chief, said Infantino had proposed “a bad deal for Fifa’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game”. He questioned the lack of transparency in Fifa’s process and pointed out that the governing body is sitting on vast debt-free reserves that could be used to fund development.

“Why this deal?” he asked. “Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?”

But an extraordinary statement later in the day by Kevin Lamour, Fifa’s current chief operating officer, may have inflicted a more serious wound. Lamour, a close associate of Infantino at Fifa and during their previous spells at Uefa, said staff and other stakeholders had been “deceived” by the president and said he would tolerate being sacked for expressing his views.

“What has been announced in recent days and what has been happening behind the scenes in recent months defies belief and imagination,” Lamour said. “To put it very clearly and directly: the project that has sparked so much controversy and debate is not a Fifa project. It is even less a project of Fifa’s administration. It is the project of one person.

“The Fifa vice-presidents, the members of the Fifa Council, the confederations, the federations, the players, the leagues, the clubs, and the fans were not the only ones who were ignored. Fifa’s own administration was also deceived.

“This lie by omission over many months and this unilateral exercise of power are not trivial. They are indicative of a lack of trust, a lack of transparency, a lack of discernment, a lack of good governance. And a serious lack of respect.”

Lamour said Fifa’s mission is “not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies Fifa when he is supposed to be at its service”. He stated that his colleagues “deserve better than contempt and intimidation”, adding: “My feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for Fifa, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us.”

Infantino appears to be shedding allies and there was no succour to be taken from a strongly worded statement from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which backed Uefa and Concacaf in their opposition to the privately funded Fifa Forward Enterprise plan. The AFC stopped short of matching Uefa’s boycott but was clear in saying the proposal should be scrapped.

“The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a Fifa World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone who cares about the future of our game,” it said. “The AFC believes that the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward.”

It called upon Fifa to “undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework”, echoing its peers’ complaints about a lack of consultation regarding key decisions such as World Cup hosting arrangements.

A further revelation on Friday that Fifa has opened a tender for research companies to assess the economic benefits of expanding the World Cup to 64 teams , demanding a hugely accelerated timescale, has only increased such concerns in football’s corridors of power.

Uefa is minded to play a waiting game after securing a united front in opposing Infantino’s plan. It will assess how Fifa reacts, although early signs suggest little change of tack. Overnight Fifa had attempted to blame media reporting for such widespread opposition, claiming its commitment to “an open and democratic consultation”, although that intervention has cut no ice among its opponents.

It is unlikely any mechanism to depose Infantino will be triggered immediately although in theory an extraordinary Fifa Congress, and subsequent vote of confidence, could be convened if 43 countries make such a request. The priority around Uefa and beyond is to see off the FFE plan before taking further steps. Any Europe-backed candidate for the Fifa presidency election in March is likely to hail from a different continent, with the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, and AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa, among possible contenders. The latter lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 election .

Late on Friday night the South American soccer body ⁠Conmebol said it had ⁠requested further ⁠information ​from Fifa on its proposal to ⁠sell a stake in its tournament business, including ⁠the World Cup, and ​launched ‌a consultation ‌process with its member ‌associations.

Conmebol said it had requested further information and clarifications from Fifa on the proposal’s scope, structure, ‌governance and potential effects, and would continue ​to analyse it before taking a position.

“We recognise that the development ⁠of football requires commercial and ​financial ​decisions. However, ​such decisions must always ​serve ‌football ​and ​never take precedence over its very essence,” Conmebol said in a statement.

articles.title: $2m crime novel deal collapses amid questions over AI use
articles.summary: Agents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’ A high-profile publishing deal for a debut crime novel has collapsed after doubts emerged over whether artificial intelligence played a role in writing it. The hotly anticipated manuscript Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body, by Jerry Falade, was withdrawn from sale by its agent despite reportedly receiving an offer for more than $2m (£1.5m) from Minotaur, owned by Macmillan US, as part of a 14-way auction. articles.content:
Agents withdraw Jerry Falade’s hotly anticipated debut after saying they can no longer authenticate ‘how the manuscript evolved’

A high-profile publishing deal for a debut crime novel has collapsed after doubts emerged over whether artificial intelligence played a role in writing it.

The hotly anticipated manuscript Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body, by Jerry Falade, was withdrawn from sale by its agent despite reportedly receiving an offer for more than $2m (£1.5m) from Minotaur, owned by Macmillan US, as part of a 14-way auction. The plan was to publish it in 2028.

An email sent to publishers by Falade’s agents and seen by the Guardian said: “Jerry Falade produced an incredible manuscript that dazzled us and the top publishing professionals around the world. Unfortunately, we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion.”

It continued: “During the submission process we vetted the manuscript with Jerry for AI and felt trusting in his reassurance that it was written without utilising AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book.”

The US auction was run by the author’s agent Marc Gerald of Europa Content, according to the Bookseller. In the UK, Sandy Hodgman of Hodgman Literary is said to have secured several six-figure bids through a similarly competitive process. The Guardian has approached both agents for comment.

Gerald told the Bookseller he first read the book in June, and that it was “stunningly good, everyone fell in love with it. It’s a book that appeals to absolutely everyone.”

He said that halfway through the submissions process, an editor raised concerns that the book had signs of potential AI use. Gerald said Europa opted against using AI-detection software to check the manuscript, saying Falade was “clear and credible” in his explanation.

However, after a meeting on 29 July, when “aspects of [Falade’s] story changed”, the agency decided to cut ties, citing the “need to have total faith”.

“We feel terrible for putting this into the universe and the firestorm it has caused,” Gerald added. “The book itself is genius – however it came to be drafted, it’s amazing.”

Falade’s case is the latest in a string of controversies to hit publishing this year, as authors, agents and publishers grapple with how to handle suspected AI use in manuscripts. Earlier this year, Hachette pulled the US release of Mia Ballard’s horror novel Shy Girl after rumours circulated online that the author had relied on AI, something she denies.

In a statement to the Guardian, Falade rejected claims that he had used AI and said the response reflected racial bias in publishing.

He said: “Three Black authors received major publishing deals this year, and all three later had deals cancelled or disrupted following suspicions about AI. There seems to be a troubling assumption that when a Black writer produces work that attracts significant attention, the work could not possibly be their own. Meanwhile, there are popular white writers who have publicly mentioned using AI for their writing processes and they’re still doing fine.”

Falade did not name other authors, but two Black authors in the US – Ballard and HM Wolfe, author of the viral romance Daggermouth – faced allegations of AI use this year. Wolfe also denies she used AI.

Falade said: “In my case, rumours began circulating and, within six hours, I had been dropped by my agency, deals were paused, and press releases were being issued.” He added that AI-detection tools “are widely known to produce false positives”. He said the novel had “passed through first readers, second readers, editors, and acquisitions teams at numerous publishing houses … If the manuscript had shown genuine signs of being generated by AI, it is difficult to believe that every one of those experienced professionals would have failed to notice.”

articles.content:
From sea swimming to painting, doctors are ‘prescribing’ hobbies – but you don’t need a doctor’s note to get started

In 2020, the year Amanda lost her mother, husband, job and pre-pandemic normalcy, she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder. “My life was just spiraling down and down and down,” she says.

To help with her symptoms, in addition to an antidepressant prescription, Amanda was given a “ social prescription ”: a referral to a non-medical, community-based activity, typically involving movement, nature, art or service. Amanda lives near Devon, England, and became curious about sea swimming after reading about its health benefits and watching other women do it at her local beach all year round. When she told this to her mental health nurse, she was prescribed a spot in Chill Therapy , an eight-week course that teaches swimming, floating and breathing techniques to build skill and confidence navigating the open water.

Six years later, Amanda turns to swimming in the sea whenever she feels stressed. “It invigorates me and makes me feel I can cope with anything,” she says. “I can’t do without it, to be honest.” She is now down to the lowest dose of her antidepressant, and has made a ton of friends along the way: “I feel refreshed in body and soul.”

Though research has long linked hobbies involving exercise, arts and nature to a wide range of health benefits, social prescribing now lets people like Amanda participate in them as part of their healthcare, typically covering barriers like cost and transportation. While the practice is more common in the UK, some insurers in the US are starting to participate in social prescribing.

But you don’t need a doctor’s note to get started. We asked experts in the social prescribing field for tips on picking a hobby that will actually improve your health.

When choosing a hobby, think about how you’re feeling now, and how you’d like to feel in the future.

For instance, if you’ve been feeling tired or down, like Amanda, science suggests you should move your body; for example, multiple studies show sea swimming can help reduce depression and depressive symptoms .

On a physiological level, this makes sense: aerobic exercise has been linked with gains in mood-boosting endorphins and serotonin . Additionally, time spent in nature is linked with lower levels of cortisol, a stress hormone .

Feeling distracted? Nature is also good at improving focus. According to the Attention Restoration Theory , nature is uniquely equipped to restore our depleted mental resources by providing “soft fascination”, a state of effortless focus that captures our attention without draining it. This could explain why nature has been shown to improve our executive functioning and concentration .

Creative activities can help with getting through sadness, isolation or pain. “Art is a human experience – it helps folks get out of their loneliness and into a flow state , which can rewire their brain from trauma,” says Holly Jacobson, CEO of Path With Art, a Seattle-based non-profit that offers free arts-based community programming. A new small study found that Path with Art participants experienced statistically significant gains in mental wellbeing and efficacy, and reductions in loneliness. Earlier small studies found that painting can reduce anxiety , and that art-making can reduce cortisol levels after 45 minutes .

Some people can’t see themselves knitting, while others might rule out sports because of injury. Research suggests we are more likely to follow through on an activity if we have intrinsic motivation – the internal drive to do something because we find it genuinely enjoyable or satisfying, rather than an external reward, like losing weight.

That’s what worked for Amanda. Instead of receiving a finger-wagging recommendation to exercise, she says she was intrinsically motivated to go sea swimming. “When I could not go in the sea while waiting for hip replacement for two years, I used to picture myself in the waves with my friends and it always cheered me up,” she says.

To help uncover a patient’s intrinsic motivation, professionals called link workers are tasked with listening to patients and helping them uncover their unique curiosities. Many are trained in motivational interviewing, an evidence-based, person-centered conversational technique that helps people work within their own value system and reasons for change, says Dr Tim Anstiss, a medical doctor who helped to develop the training, which recommends questions like: how might your life change if you joined that group? Who or what gives your life meaning and purpose?

Doing what gives us purpose and meaning is “vital” to our health and wellbeing, agrees Dr Ivory Rose, a California-based occupational therapist and lead within Social Prescribing USA. “Leisure pursuits are a very important part of [our health], but often get forgotten in the face of an illness or busy schedule,” she says, referencing studies that link meaningful activity to greater health .

Rose aims to rebuild this association for clients with questions like: what is something you used to enjoy doing that you haven’t done in a while? What is important to you to be able to do?

Mindfulness is “the very simple process of noticing”, says Dr Ellen Langer, a psychology professor at Harvard University. In her most recent book, The Mindful Body , she explores the wide-ranging benefits of being more mindful, which include improving your memory, creativity and energy, and strengthening your social relationships.

Langer says to start by noticing three new things about something familiar – say, a person, place or object. Every time you notice you are on autopilot, you build “a healthy mindset for uncertainty”, she says. This is important because people who are stressed or in pain often “believe the symptoms they have are going to stay the same or get worse”, and that suffering is constant, Langer says. But according to research, people can feel better when they notice improvements and reflect on why they feel better.

Dr Rachel Zoffness, a pain psychologist teaching at Stanford and the University of California at San Francisco, similarly points to research showing that pain can increase or decrease, depending on where we direct our attention.

In her recent book, Tell Me Where It Hurts, she offers tips for pain relief. She says she sometimes asks patients directly: “Will you tell me about a time you were so absorbed in an activity that you briefly forgot about your pain?”

If you’re not sure what brings you meaning or what captures your attention in adulthood, try reflecting on what brought you joy in childhood. “When we were kids, playing did not relate to a specific goal, but it’s the most natural form of learning,” says Purvi Shah, founder of PlayRx.life , a wellness platform. Shah advises clients to “say ‘yes’ to something new, especially when they are stuck in a rut and problems seem overwhelming”.

Caitlin Marshall, a licensed clinical social worker and co-author of Creative First Aid, agrees. In her work leading creative workshops on activities including beekeeping and watercolor painting, she focuses on helping people who are experiencing psychological distress rediscover a sense of childlike joy. “It’s about learning to help people do what feels good and inspiring to them,” she says.

Encouraging participants to be open-minded helps them to discover new things about themselves. “Some of them will arrive and say: ‘I hate cooking.’ Then those people are the ones that end up loving it,” Marshall says. “It’s hard to be judgmental and curious at the same time.”

Creative activities can help with getting through sadness, isolation or pain. “Art is a human experience – it helps folks get out of their loneliness and into a flow state , which can rewire their brain from trauma,” says Holly Jacobson, CEO of Path With Art, a Seattle-based non-profit that offers free arts-based community programming. A new small study found that Path with Art participants experienced statistically significant gains in mental wellbeing and efficacy, and reductions in loneliness. Earlier small studies found that painting can reduce anxiety , and that art-making can reduce cortisol levels after 45 minutes .

Some people can’t see themselves knitting, while others might rule out sports because of injury. Research suggests we are more likely to follow through on an activity if we have intrinsic motivation – the internal drive to do something because we find it genuinely enjoyable or satisfying, rather than an external reward, like losing weight.

That’s what worked for Amanda. Instead of receiving a finger-wagging recommendation to exercise, she says she was intrinsically motivated to go sea swimming. “When I could not go in the sea while waiting for hip replacement for two years, I used to picture myself in the waves with my friends and it always cheered me up,” she says.

To help uncover a patient’s intrinsic motivation, professionals called link workers are tasked with listening to patients and helping them uncover their unique curiosities. Many are trained in motivational interviewing, an evidence-based, person-centered conversational technique that helps people work within their own value system and reasons for change, says Dr Tim Anstiss, a medical doctor who helped to develop the training, which recommends questions like: how might your life change if you joined that group? Who or what gives your life meaning and purpose?

Doing what gives us purpose and meaning is “vital” to our health and wellbeing, agrees Dr Ivory Rose, a California-based occupational therapist and lead within Social Prescribing USA. “Leisure pursuits are a very important part of [our health], but often get forgotten in the face of an illness or busy schedule,” she says, referencing studies that link meaningful activity to greater health .
Rose aims to rebuild this association for clients with questions like: what is something you used to enjoy doing that you haven’t done in a while? What is important to you to be able to do?

Mindfulness is “the very simple process of noticing”, says Dr Ellen Langer, a psychology professor at Harvard University. In her most recent book, The Mindful Body , she explores the wide-ranging benefits of being more mindful, which include improving your memory, creativity and energy, and strengthening your social relationships.

Langer says to start by noticing three new things about something familiar – say, a person, place or object. Every time you notice you are on autopilot, you build “a healthy mindset for uncertainty”, she says. This is important because people who are stressed or in pain often “believe the symptoms they have are going to stay the same or get worse”, and that suffering is constant, Langer says. But according to research, people can feel better when they notice improvements and reflect on why they feel better.

Dr Rachel Zoffness, a pain psychologist teaching at Stanford and the University of California at San Francisco, similarly points to research showing that pain can increase or decrease, depending on where we direct our attention.

In her recent book, Tell Me Where It Hurts, she offers tips for pain relief. She says she sometimes asks patients directly: “Will you tell me about a time you were so absorbed in an activity that you briefly forgot about your pain?”

If you’re not sure what brings you meaning or what captures your attention in adulthood, try reflecting on what brought you joy in childhood. “When we were kids, playing did not relate to a specific goal, but it’s the most natural form of learning,” says Purvi Shah, founder of PlayRx.life , a wellness platform. Shah advises clients to “say ‘yes’ to something new, especially when they are stuck in a rut and problems seem overwhelming”.

Caitlin Marshall, a licensed clinical social worker and co-author of Creative First Aid, agrees. In her work leading creative workshops on activities including beekeeping and watercolor painting, she focuses on helping people who are experiencing psychological distress rediscover a sense of childlike joy. “It’s about learning to help people do what feels good and inspiring to them,” she says.

Encouraging participants to be open-minded helps them to discover new things about themselves. “Some of them will arrive and say: ‘I hate cooking.’ Then those people are the ones that end up loving it,” Marshall says. “It’s hard to be judgmental and curious at the same time.”

articles.title: Luxury is coming for our teeth – but should we really be paying £20 for a tube of toothpaste?

articles.content:
Minty fresh flavours are out, gold plated toothbrushes are in, and dental experts are sceptical

F irst it came for handwash. Then deodorant. Now, the fancification trend has claimed its next victim: dental products. From £20 toothpastes to bottles of mouthwash that sound more like a perfume than a breath freshener, a new wave of oral care is blurring the lines between function and fashion.

Rather than being shoved in an old tumbler on the back of the shelf, today’s iterations of toothbrushes and pastes are at the forefront of social media sink shots , proudly displayed alongside a three-wick candle and curated pile of skincare.

A recent report from the marketing insights firm VLM described the mouth in grander terms than we’re perhaps, used to, calling it “the new centre of gravity for beauty, longevity and self-expression”, and highlighting a shift in oral care from “a hygiene necessity into a pillar of holistic wellness”.

With the emergence of brands that treat toothpaste more like a perfume, mint is no longer the default flavour. The French brand Le Bon works with an aroma house in Grasse to create its offering, which includes everything from blackcurrant to rose and orange blossom in packaging that could be mistaken for a hand cream. The Swedish brand Selahatin even includes flavour notes in its descriptions. It recently teamed up with the fashion designer Rick Owens on a limited-edition line of products including a toothpaste with top notes of Madagascan vanilla and base of black pepper, which it describes as capturing “the quiet act of transformation”.

Unsurprisingly, what you pop your pea-size amount of toothpaste on has also become a signifier. Apirori sells brushes with asymmetric bristle pads, designed for effective cleaning of the tooth surface, but its striking colour choices and signature gold accent are just as arresting. The Swiss brand Aurezzi takes it one step further with 24k gold-plated handles, yours for £49. Elsewhere, Machete sells brushes hand-sculpted from Italian acetate, which it describes as a “design moment for your bathroom”, while vintage fans will love Acca Kappa’s retro designs . On the cheaper end of the scale, Curaprox’s £5.90 brushes come in a range of 31 different colours. Electric toothbrushes are also pivoting from harsh whites to gentle pastel shades that look soothing rather than shouty in a bathroom shelfie.

Dr Brandon Nejati, founder of the Nejati Clinic in London, says the trend shows how wellness is encroaching all parts of our daily routines. “People are no longer looking at the body in isolation,” he says. “They increasingly understand that the mouth is not separate from overall health, but one of the body’s most important protective barriers and a gateway to the rest of the body.” Along with his co-founder and wife, Dr Mahsa Nejati, the duo have developed their own range of oral products, Mahsa, that consists of toothpastes and mouthwashes that they say aim to “support the oral microbiome, reduce inflammation and promote long-term oral wellness”.

Nejati says the trend is helping to change the way people think about dental care. “People are far more likely to maintain habits that feel enjoyable, thoughtful and purposeful,” he says. Selahatin’s founder, Kristoffer Vural, meanwhile describes the brand as transforming “the most ordinary act into a rite of taste, memory and emotion”, which is certainly something to mull over during your two minutes of brushing.

The trend is also having a knock-on effect on the dentist chair with clinics offering treatments beyond the basic polish and scale. Many now provide LED light therapy and lasers that may help reduce inflammation, while others offer complementary treatments such as acupuncture that may help with jaw issues.

“For decades, oral care was largely focused on preventing cavities or whitening teeth,” Nejati says. “Today, there is growing recognition that maintaining a healthy oral microbiome, reducing chronic inflammation and preserving the integrity of the oral barrier may have implications far beyond the mouth. As the science has evolved, so too has consumer awareness.”

However, with many people in the UK struggling to even get basic dental treatment due to a scarcity of NHS dentists , the maintenance of a smile is quickly becoming an even brighter status symbol.

Not every dental expert is thrilled with this new luxury or holistic spin. Some upscale toothpaste brands, such as the US-founded label Theodent , don’t contain fluoride, which the British Dental Association cautions against. “The introduction of fluoride toothpaste in the mid-20th century has had a transformative impact on oral health in the UK by significantly reducing tooth decay rates,” says its chair, Eddie Crouch. “It achieves this by remineralising weakened enamel, slowing mineral loss, and hindering plaque bacteria acids. The BDA would not recommend any toothpaste without it.”

Crouch is also critical of the trend’s high price tags. “You can find perfectly decent toothpaste at a pound shop,” says Crouch. “Ultimately the deciding factor isn’t whether your next tube comes with ‘notes of vanilla’, but whether it has the necessary fluoride to protect your teeth.”

Nejati compares the trend to skincare where the efficacy varies widely. “Elevating the daily experience encourages consistency, but the products must also deliver genuine scientific value,” he says. “The difference should never simply be branding – it should be the underlying science, formulation and philosophy. If a product is genuinely designed to support the oral microbiome, help reduce inflammation, preserve the oral barrier and encourage healthier long-term habits, then it represents a fundamentally different proposition.”

But perhaps dental experts shouldn’t be too concerned. Just like Aesop handsoap pump bottles are often refilled with cheaper dupes, it appears some dental products may be treated as for display purposes only. In a Reddit thread dedicated to the Rick Owens x Selahatin collaboration, one user wrote: “I treat it more like a collectible.” They’re not the only one. Despite the manual toothbrush priced at £50 and toothpaste at £40, both items are now out of stock and fetching triple their original prices on resale sites. Expect to find them pride of place (and most likely unused) in the fanciest bathrooms sometime soon.

articles.title: How police are trying to divert teen hackers away from crime
articles.summary: Cyber Prevent is targeting predominantly boys and young men at risk of being drawn to cyber criminality.
articles.content:
Lucas was 16 when he got into trouble for hacking his school computers. Twice.

He wanted access to play games and visit blocked websites so he started tinkering with programming.

At one point he even unscrewed the computer tower to take some internal components home for tests.

"It's quite a sense of achievement when you've succeeded in doing something that two or three trained professionals have spent a lot of time trying to stop you doing," he said.

He was close to being expelled - but his worried mother had no idea how serious his actions were.

She called the police and invited an officer from the nationwide programme Cyber Choices to their home in rural Cumbria.

"My mum was like, 'ooh, you've got a detective coming to speak to you, you're in a lot of trouble'," Lucas said.

"So I was sat at the window waiting. Who's going to come? How much trouble am I going to be in?"

PC Sam Cooper knocked on the door earlier this year and has been working with Lucas ever since.

PC Sam Cooper visits children at their homes to guide them away from cyber-crime

He explained to Lucas, as he has with dozens of other children, there were real consequences and harm caused by cyber-attacks.

Cooper said showing the mostly teenage boys what was legal and not was step one.

Then comes positive encouragement over months of one-to-one meetings, usually at their homes.

"I'll try and find where their interests are and try and divert them towards professional training, qualifications," he said.

Cyber Choices, also known as Cyber Prevent, is like a hacker rehab course.

It works in parallel with the more well-known Prevent scheme, which identifies potential terror offenders.

While at Lucas's house I saw first hand how some of the conversations work.

Lucas enthusiastically explained his latest computer experiments and Cooper asked him what software and tools he was using to check they were legitimate.

Soon the officer will take Lucas on a visit to the local university where he will be shown the cyber security course with the aim of inspiring him to apply.

Paul Foster, the NCA's cyber prevention lead, says hacking has become "more of a problem"

More than 1,150 cases have been referred to the National Crime Agency (NCA)'s Cyber Choices scheme in the last eight years - nearly 600 of those were in the last three years.

Authorities warn teenage hacking groups are playing an increasingly prominent role in serious cyber-attacks.

Young, English-speaking hackers have been linked to attacks on major organisations including Transport for London (TfL) and MGM Grand in 2024, and Marks & Spencer and the Co-op in 2025.

Individuals are also being increasingly targeted in hacks for their cryptocurrency holdings.

"It certainly has become more of a problem," said Paul Foster, who leads cyber prevention work at the NCA.

"Certainly English-speaking, Western world individuals that we know are now more active in cyber-crime."

He said young people were engaged with online activity and devices at increasingly young ages exposing them to criminal communities and influences.

Police say many young offenders do not initially set out to become criminals.

Instead, they often begin by experimenting with technology, testing systems or trying to bypass restrictions before becoming drawn into online communities where hacking is encouraged.

The children can come from all over the country and from a range of backgrounds, and Cooper said many be autistic or are neurodiverse.

"The vast majority of individuals I'm dealing with are neurodiverse," he said.

"Even if they're not labelled as such... they obviously have more affinity with computers than they do with practical and social reality," he said.

"Sometimes they can get fixated on certain goals and not listen to any adults around them, so that's where I come in and sit them down and talk to them."

In 2023, a high profile teenage hacker called Arion Kurtaj, who had hacked Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games, was deemed unfit to stand trial because he was severely autistic.

Two teenage hackers who were jailed earlier this month for the TfL hack were also autistic - which was taken into account by the judge when he sentenced them to five and a half years in prison.

One of them, Owen Flowers from Walsall, had been offered a chance to enrol on the Cyber Choices programme when he first got into trouble shortly after he turned 16.

Some critics argue that teaching cyber skills to young people who have already shown an interest in hacking risks making them more capable offenders.

In another ongoing court case, it emerged a teenager who had been enrolled on the programme was alleged to have gone on to commit further offences.

Foster said he understood the concern but believes the alternative would be worse.

"My fear is that if we didn't give them something like Cyber Choices, where would they get that input and where would that input take them?"

The NCA hopes it could intervene before curiosity, talent and online influence turn into serious offending.

For Lucas, the fear of having a police officer show up at his door made him rethink things.

He admits that if he had not been caught and helped by the scheme he would have carried on pushing boundaries in his exploration of computers and hacking.

Meanwhile in Leicestershire, 21-year-old cyber-security professional Izak is another Cyber Choices success story.

At 15, he hacked his school computers so he could make graphic designs in Photoshop, but he also found himself drawn into cyber-crime groups online who were making "lots of money".

A visit from Leicestershire Police got him on to the programme and helped him see cyber-security as a possible job opportunity, by encouraging him to "use my cyber skills for good".

articles.title: ‘I was hyperventilating and sobbing’: Tomi Adeyemi says Children of Blood and Bone film ‘the worst thing I’ve ever lived through’
articles.summary: Author of books behind forthcoming film starring Viola Davis and Idris Elba appears to have had disagreement with cast member Amandla Stenberg Tomi Adeyemi, the author of Children of Blood and Bone , has spoken further on the difficult process behind adapting her novel for this big screen, calling it “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”. articles.content:
Author of books behind forthcoming film starring Viola Davis and Idris Elba appears to have had disagreement with cast member Amandla Stenberg

Tomi Adeyemi, the author of Children of Blood and Bone , has spoken further on the difficult process behind adapting her novel for this big screen, calling it “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”.

In a five-minute video on TikTok, the author said she left the set of the Paramount production “hyperventilating and sobbing”, adding: “I never want to hear about this project again”.

Adeyemi, who co-wrote the screenplay for the film, had previously spoken about her concerns surrounding the adaptation, saying that she wasn’t intending to watch the film.

The video she posted on TikTok was intended, she said, to try to put the affair to bed, although the author conceded it might prolong the story. She also said that the people involved with the film had continued to “antagonise” her.

“What I’m about to share is not a secret to the people involved,” she said. “It’s a reality that I’ve had to live with for about a year and a half, and everyone involved, at least at the highest level, has been made aware of this reality, and they haven’t done anything to make it better. If anything, they’ve only antagonised me, and I accept that. But I also accept if I don’t say something, I think it’s just going to be worse.”

She continued: “I’m not going to speak on what I endured to make it through the young adult trilogy, and I’m not going to speak about everything that I also suffered through or endured to make the adaptation a reality.

“I’m actually only going to speak about what happened after I left that set of my own film adaptation, hyperventilating and sobbing. There are many witnesses, so it’s not really a secret. I came back to America and suffered such severe somatic pain and so many panic attacks. I knew it was so bad that I would never ever be able to watch this film, and I made peace with that.”

Speaking to the Los Angeles Times earlier this week, director Gina Prince-Bythewood appeared to allude to a casting controversy involving Amandla Stenberg, who portrays Princess Amari in the film.

articles.content:
Tech workers are increasingly unionizing, trading Silicon Valley’s myth of exceptionalism for collective bargaining to contest the corporate deployment of artificial intelligence

F or decades, the technology industry was a fortress that labor unions couldn’t breach. Tech workers already had cushy compensation packages, dream benefits like unlimited vacation and free lunch, and a flat corporate hierarchy that made engineers feel as powerful as their bosses, all of whom dressed down in sneakers and hoodies. So why unionize?

Now, that fortress is cracking from the inside. Unions have become increasingly popular for tech employees. After months of mass layoffs tied to artificial intelligence and mounting anxieties about how it’s being deployed, some tech workers say they’ve been saddled with higher workloads while facing the threat of job loss caused by the very products they’re building. Workers from Google DeepMind and Meta in the UK are also objecting to how their companies’ AI products are being used, such as for military purposes or to monitor employee productivity . Those same workers are now attempting to unionize.

On the frontlines of AI’s rollout in the workplace, tech workers have often been the first to feel its effects – including job loss, employee surveillance , increasing workloads, and uses that conflict with employees’ values. These problems aren’t unique to software companies, though, and how Silicon Valley workers fare could serve as a bellwether for what’s coming as AI spreads to other industries.

A Meta employee who was part of a recent union drive in the UK said, “It’s about us having a voice in all of the operations of the company, from products to employee experience.” The employee spoke to the Guardian on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal from their employer.

After Meta cut thousands of workers in May and piloted a program tracking their activities, some employees felt power had tipped toward their employer. Forming a union, the Meta employee said, “is the best way to actually show up as owners, and take our seat at the table”.

The push toward tech unionization has been building for years and includes workers at the crowdfunding platform Kickstarter and Microsoft-owned gaming company ZeniMax, as well as the Alphabet Workers Union (AWU), which represents more than 1,400 workers across Google, YouTube and Waymo.

The latest AI-driven developments will drive more organizing efforts, AWU predicts. In the past year, participation in collective actions like AWU’s job security petition , which garnered 4,500 signatures and was delivered to executives last week, increased. Total union actions at Alphabet doubled in 2025 from the year prior.

“In the age of AI, workers need a real say within our companies now more than ever,” said Emma Jackson, senior staff program manager and AWU communications chair. Strong participation “shows workers’ increasing willingness to take a stand and strengthen their agency”.

In a statement, Google DeepMind said it was in the “early stages” of the process to recognize the union and plans to “continue to engage in good faith”. Meta didn’t comment.

As companies continue to cut, tech workers face a stark reality sharply at odds with the job security they once took for granted. “When I first started in tech, you could leave a job and have another one by the week with better pay,” said John Chadfield, a former tech worker who co-founded United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW), the UK’s only union specifically for tech industry workers. Now, engineers are realizing they don’t have as much power as they once thought, he said. “You might be well paid, but you are still workers.”

“This sense of privilege and immunity for tech workers – that is gone,” said Simone Robutti, a member of Tech Workers Coalition, an international grassroots tech labor network that’s been growing as companies restructure around AI. “It’s clear that with very few exceptions, tech workers are as replaceable as other workers.”

Meanwhile, employees using AI aren’t necessarily experiencing the efficiency boosts the tech promised to deliver. In a recent survey of information technology workers across the University of California campuses, 65% of people reported taking on more work due to a vacant position. Managers expect AI to fill some of those gaps, but people just end up doing more work, said Max Belasco, a business systems analyst at the University of California, Los Angeles chool of Law and union member. And despite the additional responsibility, only 22% of people said they felt secure in their jobs, the survey showed.

“We want to see the UC embody a new way of approaching technology that isn’t just an echo of the consultant-driven layoffs that you see inside of Silicon Valley or the idea that AI can just be this cost-cutting measure,” he said.

University spokesperson Heather Hansen said the school system was focused on using AI “thoughtfully and responsibly to strengthen its operations”. Decisions about how it uses AI are guided by “operational needs” and “privacy, security, and policy considerations”, she said.

The proliferation of AI is spurring workers outside the tech industry to take a similar tack. National Nurses United, which represents nurses in the US, has fought against the use of AI in clinical settings; Sag-Aftra, which represents workers in media and Hollywood, pushed back on the use of AI to replace creative workers in film.

Unions aren’t the only way to set up these kinds of guardrails, but “when employees begin organizing, it’s often a signal that they don’t feel heard through the channels that already exist,” said Katie Hawkes, an organizational psychologist whose doctoral research focused on tech labor union participation.

She witnessed this during her time at X, where employees spoke up about ethical issues like hate speech on the platform but lacked the means to pressure management. “Ultimately, like every company, leadership retained complete decision-making authority,” she said.

Still, for years, tech workers resisted unions. Chadfield said he started trying to organize tech workers a decade ago, but no one seemed interested. Workers felt reasonably happy, and “in the conversations I was having with people then, it was just like, ‘That’s a ridiculous idea. We don’t need one,’” he said.

Then, in 2018, thousands of Google employees organized to protest against the company’s involvement in Project Maven, a Pentagon initiative that used machine learning to analyze drone footage. The action was surprisingly effective, and Google dropped the contract months later, though Palantir picked it up and continues it to this day. A few years later, in 2021, Google employees formed the Alphabet Workers Union. In 2022, Amazon warehouse workers also formed a union, which the company has fought tooth and nail to not formally recognize.

Within the last few years, though, Chadfield said white-collar workers were increasingly interested in union representation – even at companies like Meta, where he said UTAW did not previously have any members. “Until recently, [Meta] was kind of the very last bastion of that Silicon Valley-ness,” he said. “Now, we’re getting a lot of members from Meta, and that’s not something we ever expected.”

Unions can offer workers significant protections. ZeniMax, the Microsoft-owned game company, unionized in 2023 and finalized a contract for its quality assurance testers in 2025 that included protections relating to AI usage, outsourcing and overtime. In summer, when Microsoft cut thousands of jobs, including some at ZeniMax, severance benefits were spelled out in the contract.

“Building even simple protections over issues like job security is an ongoing effort,” said Autumn Mitchell, a quality assurance tester who was laid off by ZeniMax. “Having a union means having negotiating rights over issues like layoffs, which is more than what a lot of people are working with right now in game development.”

Kickstarter, which formed one of the first company-wide tech unions in 2020, negotiated a new contract in 2025 that included a four-day workweek, a minimum salary for all workers, protections against replacing full-time workers with contractors, and an agreement that management cannot replace roles with AI. Though some employees were skeptical of organizing six years ago, its latest win is an example of what can be achieved with a strong union, Robutti of Tech Workers Coalition Global said. And it’s a lesson that applies beyond the tech industry.

“The best time to unionize was always yesterday,” he said. “The second best time is today.”

They want to connect and give back to their communities. But volunteering, much like Sunday meal prep or morning meditations , often ends up at the bottom of the to-do list – a nice idea we’ll get to when we have more time. “For many people, volunteering is something they feel positively about, but don’t always prioritize or think they have time for,” says Matt Bertram, vice-president of volunteer services for the American Red Cross. How to start meditating How to start weightlifting How to start budgeting How to start running Continue reading...
articles.content:
Common misconceptions are that you don’t have the right skills, or you need to make a huge time commitment

M any people want to do good in the world. They want to connect and give back to their communities. But volunteering, much like Sunday meal prep or morning meditations , often ends up at the bottom of the to-do list – a nice idea we’ll get to when we have more time.

“For many people, volunteering is something they feel positively about, but don’t always prioritize or think they have time for,” says Matt Bertram, vice-president of volunteer services for the American Red Cross.

Common misconceptions about volunteering, he says, are that you don’t have the right skills to contribute, or that you have to make a huge time commitment.

“In reality, there are many flexible volunteer roles to fit all interests and skill sets,” he says.

There are mental and physical benefits to volunteering. According to a 2023 paper , these include reduced mortality and increased functioning, as well as less tangible benefits like increased quality of life, pride, empowerment, motivation, social support and sense of community.

First, think about the causes or issues you care about. And think broadly.

“The sense of what counts as volunteering has shifted,” says Boram Kim, vice-president for volunteer and institutional engagement at Habitat for Humanity International. Volunteering is no longer limited to traditional, formal roles through large, international organizations. “Increasingly, people mobilize around smaller, immediate issues close to home and within their own communities,” she explains.

After Covid arrived, the number of mutual aid organizations in the US ballooned from 50 to 800, according to the National Education Association . These groups are diverse: some run food pantries, while others help with disaster relief or exchange services and resources. Find a group in your area through directories like Mutual Aid Hub in the US, or Mutual Aid in the UK.

Whether you’re interested in volunteering with a large organization or a small local group, consider your motivation and what you hope to gain from the experience.

“For some, it’s a chance to build skills or strengthen their community, while for others it’s about social connection,” says Kim. “The most essential thing to consider is [the organization’s] alignment with the issues that matter more to [the volunteer].”

As you look at groups and organizations that appeal to you, be realistic about how much time and energy you can offer.

“Keep in mind that every organization has unique needs,” says Julie Sonenberg, senior manager of volunteer engagement at the ASPCA Adoption Center. “Try to find alignment with what you’re able to contribute and what the organization’s needs are.”

When you find a group or organization you like, check their website for volunteer signup information or, if this doesn’t exist, send them an email expressing your interest and availability.

“Once people have a good idea of where and how they want to volunteer, they shouldn’t be afraid to reach out to organizations they are passionate about,” says Kyle Gardner, senior vice-president of development at Charity Navigator.

If you ultimately don’t have the time to volunteer, Gardner suggests contributing in other ways, like setting up recurring donations to a charity, or donating items like food, clothes or furniture.

“One mistake people make when it comes to volunteering is underestimating their skills,” says Kim. People often assume they need specific expertise or skills to contribute, when in fact, “compassion and reliability are the most valuable assets”, he says.

Volunteering can involve hands-on work, but some roles focus on advocacy, fundraising, digital support or storytelling.

At the ASPCA, for example, people often assume “opportunities to volunteer are only available inside a shelter”, Sonenberg says. Such opportunities may entail walking dogs, folding laundry, greeting visitors or cleaning. But the organization also needs advocacy volunteers to help mobilize people and improve laws for animals, and first responders to help animals in crisis.

Many non-profit organizations – including some large, well-known organizations, like the American Red Cross – depend on volunteers to operate. “About 90% of our workforce are volunteers,” Bertram says.

Contributing to a blood drive, supporting community-preparedness events or serving in a virtual or on-call role all make a difference. “Some volunteers contribute just a few hours a month, and that support still makes a real difference,” he says.

Volunteering is also a good reminder that, as helpless as we may feel, our actions can make a difference.

“In my work, I see volunteers transform just as much as the communities they serve,” he says. “Volunteering is a pathway to connection, to each other, to our communities, and to the belief that we can shape a better world.”

Volunteering can involve hands-on work, but some roles focus on advocacy, fundraising, digital support or storytelling.

At the ASPCA, for example, people often assume “opportunities to volunteer are only available inside a shelter”, Sonenberg says. Such opportunities may entail walking dogs, folding laundry, greeting visitors or cleaning. But the organization also needs advocacy volunteers to help mobilize people and improve laws for animals, and first responders to help animals in crisis.

Many non-profit organizations – including some large, well-known organizations, like the American Red Cross – depend on volunteers to operate. “About 90% of our workforce are volunteers,” Bertram says.

Contributing to a blood drive, supporting community-preparedness events or serving in a virtual or on-call role all make a difference. “Some volunteers contribute just a few hours a month, and that support still makes a real difference,” he says.
Volunteering is also a good reminder that, as helpless as we may feel, our actions can make a difference.

“In my work, I see volunteers transform just as much as the communities they serve,” he says. “Volunteering is a pathway to connection, to each other, to our communities, and to the belief that we can shape a better world.”
